# SequenceLink

> SequenceLink is an open-source framework for serving robot policies from remote GPUs over wide-area networks (Python,
> Apache-2.0): a policy written as a `@seq.policy` class and served with `seq serve` on the GPU,
> `sequence_ai.connect(address)` on the robot, every default on.
> Its inference layer (`sequence_ai.engine`) and its network layer (`sequence_ai.network`) also work in any policy
> server: each component is one file that is used independently in an existing server or robot program, most of them
> standard library only (`optimize` needs torch 2.4 or later, or JAX).

This file is https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai's README and documentation in one piece, written by tools/make_llms_full.py.
The map of the repository, file by file, is https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/llms.txt.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/README.md

SequenceLink serves robot policies from GPUs anywhere: the policy runs on a GPU, and the robot connects to it over
the internet. Its package is `sequence-ai`. It works with openpi, LeRobot, GR00T and Octo policies, and with any policy
written as a class.

- **The GPU** runs your policy with `seq serve`. It answers each robot with a chunk of actions, can batch robots that ask
  at the same time (`@seq.concurrent`), and speeds the model up without changing its outputs.
- **The robot** connects with `connect()`. It streams its cameras as low-latency video and plays the actions, asking
  for the next chunk before the current one runs out.

## How it fits together

**`sequence_ai.network`** is the connection between a robot and the GPU its policy runs on. On the robot, `connect()`
applies the client-side components to one connection, and `openpi.keep()` does the same on the connection that openpi's
own client holds. On the server, `one_write` and `ping` wrap a uvicorn or a WebSocket server. **`sequence_ai.engine`**
is the inference layer on the GPU: `seq serve` serves a policy with the server's side of both layers on, `optimize`
shortens one inference with the speed-ups that keep its outputs exactly the same, `batcher` and `slack` share a GPU among robots, and `replicas` runs one process per GPU. **`bench/`** measures a link before anything is added to it.

## Install

```bash
pip install sequence-ai
```

The same package goes on the GPU and on the robot: Python 3.10 or later, on Linux or macOS. The speed-ups use your
model's own torch (2.4 or later) or JAX.

## Quick start

**On the GPU**, save this as `policy.py` in a folder of its own:

```python
import numpy as np
import seq


@seq.policy(hz=15, action_chunk_valid_len=8, action_chunk_replan_at=5)
class QuickstartPolicy_user:
    @seq.sample
    def sample_user(self):
        observation_user = {"image": np.zeros((224, 224, 3), dtype=np.uint8), "state": np.zeros(7, dtype=np.float32)}
        return [("observe", observation_user), ("act",)] * 3          # an observation, then an act, three times

    @seq.infer
    def infer_user(self, observation_user):
        frame_user = observation_user["image"]                       # your model here: the next 10 steps, 7 joints each
        return {"actions": np.full((10, 7), float(frame_user.mean()), dtype=np.float32)}
```

Then serve it from that folder:

```bash
seq serve
```

```text
serving quickstart-policy-user on port 8000, each robot held and seated by its time at 15 Hz: a robot connects with sequence_ai.connect("http://<this machine>:8000")
```

**On the robot**:

```python
import numpy as np
import sequence_ai

with sequence_ai.connect("http://127.0.0.1:8000") as policy_user:     # your GPU's address
    policy_user.wait_until_ready()                                     # once, before the robot moves
    frame_user = np.zeros((224, 224, 3), dtype=np.uint8)               # your camera's frame, streamed as video
    policy_user.observe({"image": sequence_ai.Video(frame_user), "state": np.zeros(7, dtype=np.float32)})
    print(policy_user.act()["actions"].shape)                           # (10, 7)
```

The robot plays 15 steps a second (`hz`), uses the first 8 steps of each chunk (`action_chunk_valid_len`), and asks for
the next chunk at step 5 (`action_chunk_replan_at`). [Quickstart](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/quickstart.md) has the whole loop. Names ending in
`_user` are yours to change.

- **An official template**: `seq init pi05-libero my_pi05_user`, then `seq serve` in that folder
  ([how](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-a-template-on-my-own-gpu.md)).
- **Both halves on one machine**: in a clone of this repository, `seq serve examples/quickstart_policy & python examples/quickstart_robot.py`.
- **A server you already run**: [its parts](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/parts-for-a-server-you-already-run.md), one file each.
- **What is on by default**: [each part, and how to turn it off](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/what-is-on-by-default.md).
- **GPUs run for you**: deploy the same folder to [General Sequences](https://generalsequences.com/docs/deploy/).

## The problem, by layer

A robot policy built on a vision-language-action (VLA) model runs each inference on a GPU, and a robot without a
suitable GPU on board sends its observations over a WAN to a remote one. Each layer of that path has its own problem.

**The model is most of the latency.** Across thirteen model and network configurations, the model is 68 to 96% of a
request's latency. The time of one inference is therefore the main lever, and `optimize` shortens it without changing
the model's output.

**One robot leaves its GPU mostly idle.** One robot keeps a GPU busy 21 to 55% of the time, so several robots can share
one, provided that no robot's action chunk runs out while its request waits. `batcher` batches the requests that are
waiting, `slack` computes how long each may wait and how many robots a replica can serve, and `replicas` runs one
replica per GPU.

**A robot pauses, and Linux restarts its connection.** A robot executes a chunk between requests, and Linux restarts a
TCP connection's congestion window after an idle period. The upload after a pause then takes one extra round trip, at
RTTs from 12 to 101 ms. `window`, `ping` and `connect` keep the window open.

**A request carries more round trips and bytes than it needs.** A response split across writes can wait a round trip
behind a tunnel, and a camera frame is 50 to 100 KB. `one_write` sends each response in one write, `connect()` sends each
camera as video and compresses a large array only when that shortens the upload, and `frames` resizes a frame before it
is sent.

**GPUs are in short supply.** Few are near any given robot, and every millisecond of round-trip time comes out of the
slack an action chunk leaves. Getting a GPU near the robot is the routing layer, which is outside this package.

## Inference layer

| Component | What it does | To add it | Requires |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`seq serve`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/seq/serve_local.py) | Serves a `@seq.policy` class to robots elsewhere: on a thread of its own, pings answered at once, a warm-up on its `@seq.sample`, pictures and compressed arrays restored, a `@seq.concurrent` policy's acts in batches. | one command | what `pip install sequence-ai` installs |
| [`optimize`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/engine/optimize.py) | Makes a policy faster on its GPU: each speed-up is kept only when its outputs on your observations stay exactly the same and acts are at least 10% faster. `seq serve` runs it on the `@seq.sample` episode. The speed-ups that change the outputs run with the difference you accept. | nothing with `seq serve`, else one call | torch 2.4 or later and a CUDA GPU, or JAX |
| [`load`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/engine/load.py) | Reads a model's weights onto the GPU from one contiguous file in parallel reads, through the page cache where memory holds it: in about 60% of the time of a checkpoint read tensor by tensor from a cold disk, every tensor the bytes it was packed with. | one call to pack, one to load | torch for a GPU, or JAX |
| [`batcher`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/engine/batcher.py) | Batches the calls waiting for a model into one call, in the batch sizes the model lists. | one object, one `await` | nothing |
| [`replicas`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/engine/replicas.py) | Runs replicas of a model, each in its own process on the GPU assigned to it, and replaces one that dies. | one object, one `await` | nothing |
| [`slack`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/engine/slack.py) | Schedules by the slack an action chunk leaves: how many robots a replica can serve, each by its own round-trip time (RTT), how long a request may wait for a batch, and which requests are dispatched first. | a few calls in your server's loop | nothing |

```python
from sequence_ai.engine import optimize, slack
from sequence_ai.engine.batcher import Batcher
from sequence_ai.engine.replicas import ReplicaPool

optimize(model_user, examples_user)                                # 32 or more of your robot's observations
batcher_user = Batcher(model_on_a_list_user, sizes=[1, 2, 4, 8], wait_ms=2.0)
pool_user = ReplicaPool(load_user, replicas=2, devices=[0, 1])     # one replica per GPU

table_user = slack.measure(forward_of_user, sizes=[1, 2, 4])       # forward_of_user(n): one forward pass of n requests
play_user = slack.playback(hz=20, valid_len=15, replan_at=8)       # 15 valid steps, the next requested at the 8th
seating_user = slack.Seating(table_user, play_user["buffer_s"] * 1000, sizes=[1, 2, 4],
                             cycle_ms=(play_user["play_s"] - play_user["buffer_s"]) * 1000)
seats_user, over_user = seating_user.seat([("near", 30.0), ("far", 200.0)])     # (robot, its RTT in ms)
```

- **`optimize`** tries `cuda_graphs` on every module that repeats and `whole_graph` on a run's whole call, keeps
  each where the outputs stay exactly the same and acts get faster, and reports why each is on or off.
  `torch_compile`, `fused_kernels`, `tensorrt` and `precision` change the outputs and need `tolerance=`.
  [How do I make a policy faster without changing its outputs, and what does each switch change?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-make-a-policy-faster-without-changing-its-outputs.md)
- **Its graphs** speed up PyTorch policies whose time goes to launching kernels. XLA already compiles each jitted
  function of a JAX policy such as π0.5 whole and puts most of its work in command buffers, so on a JAX policy they are
  tried only when you turn them on.
  `cuda_graphs` replays each module called many times per run with the same shapes from CUDA graphs of its own eager
  kernels, and checks each new shape against eager mode byte for byte. A shape whose capture fails or differs runs in eager mode from then on. The module stays the same
  object of the same class, with its weights, `state_dict` and hooks unchanged.
  [How do I make a PyTorch robot policy faster without changing its outputs?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-make-a-pytorch-robot-policy-faster-without-changing-its-outputs.md)
- **`batcher`** dispatches a batch as soon as it is full, or `wait_ms` after its first call while the model is free.
  While the model is busy, waiting calls accumulate and are dispatched together. Only the listed sizes are used, and a
  batch in which the model raised is re-run call by call.
  [How many robots can one GPU serve?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md)
- **`replicas`** runs each replica in its own process on its own GPU, so a forward pass never blocks the server's
  event loop. `ReplicaError` is the model's own error, and the replica takes the next call. `ReplicaDied` is a process
  that has exited, and it is replaced.
  [Should I run two replicas of a policy on one GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/should-i-run-two-replicas-of-a-policy-on-one-gpu.md)
- **`slack`** computes a replica's capacity from the playback time an action chunk leaves when its robot requests
  the next one, each robot by its own RTT, and tells a server how long the open batch may wait.
  [`slack`: scheduling by the slack an action chunk leaves](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/slack.md)

[How do I use the inference components with openpi, LeRobot or GR00T?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-use-the-inference-components-with-openpi-lerobot-or-gr00t.md)

## Network layer

"Client" is the robot's program and "server" is the policy server on the GPU.

| Component | Side | What it does | Requires |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`window`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/window.py) | client | Keeps the connection's congestion window across the robot's pauses: BBR on its socket, TCP keepalive, a ping while the connection is idle. | nothing |
| [`frames`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/frames.py) | both | Resizes a frame to the policy's input size and encodes it as JPEG, and turns it back into its array on the server: what openpi's own client and server carry. | Pillow |
| [`wifi_power`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/wifi_power.py) | client | Detects Wi-Fi power saving on the robot's link and reports how to disable it. | Linux |
| [`one_write`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/one_write.py) | server | Sends each HTTP response of a uvicorn server in one write instead of three. | uvicorn |
| [`tcp_link`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/tcp_link.py) | server | Reads each client's TCP state from the server's kernel: RTT, retransmitted segments, congestion window. | Linux |
| [`ping`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/ping.py) | server | A server-side ping, so that the robot's connection is not left idle while the server can answer it: the options to pass to your server. | a WebSocket server |
| [`msgpack_io`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/msgpack_io.py) | both | Encodes observations and responses as msgpack, with numpy arrays as raw bytes. Also reads openpi's layout. | nothing |
| [`latency_stats`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/latency_stats.py) | both | Counters, gauges and latencies with their p50, p95 and p99, read as one snapshot. | nothing |

Combined, and for clients you may already use:

| | Side | What it does | Requires |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`connect`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/__init__.py) | client | `sequence_ai.connect(url)`: the same policy a deployed one's name gives, on the robot's stream to your own server: each observation as it is made, a `sequence_ai.Video` item as video, each act after them. | nothing |
| [`lines`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/_core/lines_stream.py) | client | `connect(url, lines=["eth0", "wwan0"])`: the robot's stream over each of its uplinks, each line bound to its own network interface, every observation and act on every line and the first answer used. | Linux 5.7 or macOS |
| [`check`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/check.py) | client | `python -m sequence_ai.check <url>`: which defaults are on between a robot and its server, and what the server is. | httpx |
| [`openpi`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/openpi.py) | client | The client-side components on the connection held by openpi's own client. | openpi-client |
| [`lerobot`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/lerobot.py) | both | The Zenoh setting that keeps LeRobot's remote-inference connection from going idle. | lerobot 0.7 |
| [`bench/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/tree/main/bench/) | both | Measures your own link: what a pause, a ping and a camera stream cost on it. | nothing |

```python
from sequence_ai.network import lerobot, openpi

kept_user = openpi.keep(policy_user)                              # openpi: one line on its WebsocketClientPolicy
path_user = lerobot.keep_alive_file("zenoh-keep-alive.json5")     # LeRobot 0.7: one Zenoh setting, given to both sides
```

[What does each component do?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/components.md) gives the lines to add, the reason and the measurement for each
one, and [`examples/components/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/tree/main/examples/components/) has a runnable file for each.
[How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md) |
[How do I reduce the latency of LeRobot remote inference?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-reduce-the-latency-of-lerobot-remote-inference.md)
| [How do I serve a robot policy from my own GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-serve-a-robot-policy-from-my-own-gpu.md)

## Language models

`sequence_ai.chat()` and `Conversation` (an agent's history and its tool calls) take `server="openrouter"` with your
own OpenRouter key, or the address of a server of your own with the OpenAI chat completions API:

```python
result_user = sequence_ai.chat("qwen/qwen3-next-80b-a3b-instruct", [{"role": "user", "content": "Plan the next step."}],
                               server="openrouter")      # your key in OPENROUTER_API_KEY
```

[How do I use an LLM with my own OpenRouter key?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-use-an-llm-with-my-own-openrouter-key.md)

## Results

Across thirteen model and network configurations, the time a request spends outside the model ranges from 13 to
137 ms, and its share of the latency from 4 to 32%. A remote GPU is therefore close to an on-board GPU of the same
type, and inference time is the main lever.

Inference layer:

| Component | Result | Measured on |
|---|---|---|
| `cuda_graphs` | 1.54× faster (224 → 146 ms), exactly the same outputs | GR00T N1.7's diffusion transformer, one L4 |
| `cuda_graphs` against `torch.compile` | 1.54×, against 1.45× with different outputs (inductor) and 1.00× (cudagraphs) | the same model and GPU |
| `cuda_graphs` | 6.7× faster (16.1 → 2.4 ms), byte for byte | a small model of many small kernels, one T4 |
| Batching | up to 1.78× the requests per second (5.99 → 10.66) | π0.5, one L4, batch 16 |
| `slack` | 94.1% of responses in time, against 85.7% with all robots on one replica | four robots, a model paced like a 15 Hz policy |

Network layer:

| Component | Result | Measured on |
|---|---|---|
| `window`, `ping` | an upload after a pause in 1.0 round trips, not 2.0 | a 24 KB upload, RTTs of 12 to 101 ms |
| `window`: BBR | no extra round trip after a pause, also with 1% loss | a 24 KB upload, RTT about 21 ms |
| `ping`, the server's | 1.1 to 1.25 round trips, not 3.0 | 100 KB to 1 MB after 500 ms of silence |
| `window.Warm`, the robot's ping | under 1 ms, not 303.6 ms, for an upload to arrive | 162 KB uploads 3 s apart, RTT 226 ms |
| `one_write` | 106.7 ms, not 189.7, for a response | a GET through a tunnel |
| `sequence_ai.Video` | about 2.5 KB a frame, not 921,600 bytes as an array | a 640×480 camera, a textured background and three moving discs |

[Measurements](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md) lists every command, and [`bench/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/tree/main/bench/) measures your own link.

## Repository layout

```
sequence_ai/
  engine/        inference layer: serve · optimize · load · cuda_graphs · batcher · replicas · slack
  network/       network layer
                   client: connect · window · frames · wifi_power · openpi
                   server: one_write · ping · tcp_link
                   both:   msgpack_io · latency_stats · lerobot
  chat/          chat() and Conversation: on General Sequences, or at a server of your own (server=)
  check.py       python -m sequence_ai.check: which defaults are on between a robot and its server
seq/             seq init, seq serve and seq weights get, and the decorators a policy is written with
bench/           measures a link: a TCP client and server, WebSocket, Zenoh
examples/        the quick starts, and one runnable file per component
docs/            one page per question, the measurements, the FAQ
tests/           the components' tests: Python 3.9 to 3.12, on a machine with no GPU
tools/           writes llms-full.txt
```

this README and every page of `docs/` in one file.

## A note on the numbers

Every number in this README is given with the model, the GPU or the link it was measured on, and
[Measurements](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md) lists the command behind each one. What a network component saves depends on the
link, so [`bench/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/tree/main/bench/) measures yours before you add anything. Each module's docstring states what the component
does in one sentence, why, and what was measured.

## Develop

```bash
uv venv --python 3.11
uv pip install -e ".[dev]"
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q
.venv/bin/ruff check sequence_ai/engine sequence_ai/network tests examples bench tools
```

The tests are the components', and run on Python 3.9 to 3.12 on a machine with no GPU. Each release is published here
from General Sequences' own repository: [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) has what that means for a pull request.

# Quickstart: a policy and a robot

Two short files and two commands give you a policy served from your GPU and a robot that plays its answers, asking for
the next one before it runs out. No GPU and no model are needed. The output shown is from macOS on Apple silicon with
Python 3.12; Linux behaves the same way.

## 1. Install

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install sequence-ai
```

The package brings httpx, which `connect()` uses for its connection, uvicorn, which runs the server, numpy and
zstandard for arrays, Pillow for pictures, and what the `seq` command needs (pydantic and `sequence-base`).

## 2. Write a policy

Save this as `policy.py`, in a folder of its own. It is
[`examples/quickstart_policy/policy.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/quickstart_policy/policy.py).

```python
import numpy as np
import seq


@seq.policy(hz=15, action_chunk_valid_len=8, action_chunk_replan_at=5)
class QuickstartPolicy_user:
    @seq.sample
    def sample_user(self):
        observation_user = {"image": np.zeros((224, 224, 3), dtype=np.uint8), "state": np.zeros(7, dtype=np.float32)}
        return [("observe", observation_user), ("act",)] * 3          # an observation, then an act, three times

    @seq.infer
    def infer_user(self, observation_user):
        frame_user = observation_user["image"]                       # your model here: the next 10 steps, 7 joints each
        return {"actions": np.full((10, 7), float(frame_user.mean()), dtype=np.float32)}
```

- **`@seq.policy`** says how its answers play: 15 steps a second (`hz`), the first 8 steps of each answer
  (`action_chunk_valid_len`), and the next answer asked for at step 5 (`action_chunk_replan_at`), so that it arrives
  before the 8 are played.
- **`@seq.sample`** is an episode as your robot plays it: observations and acts, in order. The server warms the model up
  on its first observation before it says it is ready; without a sample, the first robot's act is the model's first.
- **`@seq.infer`** answers the latest observation with a chunk of actions. Its first dimension is time: row `i` is the
  step to play `i` steps after the observation it answers.

## 3. Serve it

In the policy's folder:

```bash
seq serve
```

It prints:

```text
serving quickstart-policy-user on port 8000: a robot connects with sequence_ai.connect("http://<this machine>:8000")
INFO:     serving QuickstartPolicy_user.infer_user on http://0.0.0.0:8000 and http://[::]:8000 (GET /stream, POST /observe, POST /act, GET /ping, GET /example, GET /record); one observation per call
WARNING:  no token: anyone who can reach port 8000 can run the policy (serve(token=...) or $SEQ_SERVE_TOKEN asks for one)
INFO:     Started server process [68489]
INFO:     Waiting for application startup.
INFO:     Application startup complete.
INFO:     warm-up: one observation took 0.3 ms, then 0.3 ms
INFO:     ready
```

It listens on every address of this machine, and ran the policy on the sample's first observation before it said
`ready`. The warning is about the token: [Put your own model and robot in](#put-your-own-model-and-robot-in) has what
to do before a robot depends on it.

## 4. Run the robot's loop

In a second terminal, with the same environment active, save this as `quickstart_robot.py`. It is
[`examples/quickstart_robot.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/quickstart_robot.py).

```python
import sys
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

import numpy as np

import sequence_ai

HZ_USER = 15            # the policy's hz: the steps a second
VALID_USER = 8          # its action_chunk_valid_len: the steps of an answer the robot plays
REPLAN_AT_USER = 5      # its action_chunk_replan_at: the step at which the robot asks for the next answer

url_user = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "http://127.0.0.1:8000"


def observation_now_user() -> dict:
    """Your robot here: its camera's frame and its joints."""
    return {"image": np.full((224, 224, 3), 128, dtype=np.uint8), "state": np.zeros(7, dtype=np.float32)}


def move_user(step_user: np.ndarray) -> None:
    """Your robot here: one step's 7 joint targets."""


def hold_user() -> None:
    """Your robot here: hold still where it is."""


def ask_user(policy_user) -> tuple:
    """The next answer's valid steps, and when it was asked for."""
    asked_user = time.monotonic()
    return policy_user.act()["actions"][:VALID_USER], asked_user


with sequence_ai.connect(url_user) as policy_user, ThreadPoolExecutor(1) as background_user:
    policy_user.wait_until_ready()                                         # once, before the robot moves
    policy_user.observe(observation_now_user())
    chunk_user, asked_user = ask_user(policy_user)
    print(f"the first answer: {len(chunk_user)} steps of {chunk_user.shape[1]} joints, the first {chunk_user[0, :3]}")
    played_user = 0
    while played_user < 3 * HZ_USER:                                       # 3 s of steps
        started_user, next_user = time.monotonic(), None
        for i_user, step_user in enumerate(chunk_user):
            if i_user == REPLAN_AT_USER:
                next_user = background_user.submit(ask_user, policy_user)  # 1. ask early, in the background
            move_user(step_user)
            played_user += 1
            policy_user.observe(observation_now_user())                    # 2. the newest observation, each step
            time.sleep(max(0.0, started_user + (i_user + 1) / HZ_USER - time.monotonic()))   # 3. on to the next step
        try:
            chunk_user, asked_user = (next_user or background_user.submit(ask_user, policy_user)).result()
            chunk_user = chunk_user[int((time.monotonic() - asked_user) * HZ_USER):]       # 4. skip the steps passed
        except Exception:                          # 5. a dropped link, a restarted server, the policy raising:
            hold_user()                            #    hold still,
            policy_user.wait_until_ready()         #    wait until the server answers again,
            policy_user.observe(observation_now_user())
            chunk_user, asked_user = ask_user(policy_user)                                  #    and go on from here
    acts_user = policy_user.stats()["latency_us"]["act_us"]
    print(f"{played_user} steps played at {HZ_USER} a second; {acts_user['n']} answers, the slowest in "
          f"{acts_user['max'] / 1000:.1f} ms")
```

```bash
python quickstart_robot.py
```

It prints:

```text
the first answer: 8 steps of 7 joints, the first [128. 128. 128.]
49 steps played at 15 a second; 8 answers, the slowest in 53.6 ms
```

The loop is yours, and its five steps keep the robot moving at 15 steps a second, and still when it cannot:

1. **It asks early, in the background.** At step 5 of the 8 it asks for the next answer on a thread of its own, so the
   answer comes while it plays the last three.
2. **It hands over the newest observation each step**, so the next answer starts from where the robot is.
3. **It sleeps to the next step** rather than for a fixed time, so a slow `move_user` does not slow the steps down.
4. **It skips the steps that passed while the answer was on its way.** An answer's row `i` is for `i` steps after the
   observation it answered, so the rows the robot has already lived through are dropped.
5. **It holds still while the server cannot answer.** A dropped link, a restarted server or the policy raising makes
   the answer raise: the loop holds the arm, waits until the server answers again, and goes on from a fresh answer.
   The connection comes back by itself; there is nothing to connect again. With the server stopped for 2 seconds in
   the middle of a 10-second run, the loop held once, at step 35, and played on when the server was back.

The stand-in policy returns the mean of the frame it was sent, and the frame is all 128. On a Mac on Wi-Fi it also
prints one warning first: Wi-Fi power saving can hold a robot's packets back, and macOS gives nothing to check it with.

## 5. Check what is on

```bash
python -m sequence_ai.check http://127.0.0.1:8000
```

It prints:

```text
sequence-ai check: http://127.0.0.1:8000

  ok  server              sequence-ai 0.64.1, pid 68489, up 9 s, policy QuickstartPolicy_user.infer_user; it answers /ping with 200 and takes the robot's stream (x-seq-stream/3)
  ok  round trip          0.3 ms for a ping on a kept connection (median of 10); 0.0 ms for a TCP connect
  ok  send window         macOS keeps a connection's send window through pauses
  --  BBR                 macOS has no BBR, and needs none for the window
  --  Wi-Fi power saving  not checked: macOS gives nothing to read it from; this machine's requests go over Wi-Fi (en0), and a wired connection takes the question away
  ok  pings when idle     connect() pings after each 100.0 ms of idle time, and the server answers /ping with 200: the pings go on the robot's stream, from its first observation until 60 s after its last observation or act, and keep the connection, and the Wi-Fi radio, from going idle
  ok  pings in inference  answered while the model ran: 0.4 ms against 0.3 ms idle (3 pings in 3 acts)
  ok  server time         the server says it took 0.3 ms of a 1.7 ms act: 1.4 ms outside it, on the network and in this machine
  ok  first act           108.3 ms, the next ones 1.7 ms (observation from GET /example)
```

Each `ok` is a part that is on; `--` is one this machine does without, or one this run could not tell; `no` would say
what is off and why.
[What is on by default, and how do I turn each part off?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/what-is-on-by-default.md) has each part.

## What just ran

On the robot, `connect()` did what your code would otherwise have to do:

| What | Why | Component |
|---|---|---|
| Kept one stream open: each observation sent as it was made, each act after them | A new connection for each call costs a handshake each time | [`connect`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/__init__.py) |
| Requested BBR and enabled TCP keepalive, where the machine allows | Linux restarts a connection's congestion window after a pause; BBR keeps it | [`window`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/window.py) |
| Pinged the stream whenever it was idle for 100 ms | So the connection is never idle between requests | [`window`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/window.py) |
| Sent the frame as a video keyframe of its own | Far fewer bytes: the quickstart's frame, 224×224 of one color, took 834 bytes for its first frame and 247 after it, instead of 150,576 | [`markers`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/markers.py) |
| Sent the rest as msgpack, its bytes as they are | JSON carries bytes as base64, a third larger on the wire | [`msgpack_io`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/msgpack_io.py) |
| Timed every act | `policy.stats()` gives p50, p95 and p99 once there are enough samples | [`latency_stats`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/latency_stats.py) |

On the server, `seq serve` built the class, warmed it up on its sample, and ran it on a thread of its own; it answered
each ping at once, turned the keyframe back into the array the policy reads, put each response in one write
([`one_write`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/one_write.py)) and told the robot in each answer how long it took (`perf`). It
names the robot's stream (`X-Seq-Act-Formats`) and what it is (`X-Seq-Server`) on every response.

On this machine, a Mac, BBR is not available, so the connection got TCP keepalive only. On loopback none of
these components saves time: there is no network between the two programs. What each one saves on a real link is in
the README's [results](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/README.md#results).

## Put your own model and robot in

1. **Your model.** Load it in the class's `__init__` and call it in `infer_user`, which takes the observation the robot
   sent and returns what the robot needs, its first dimension time. A PyTorch model or an openpi policy goes in the
   same way: [How do I serve a robot policy from my own GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-serve-a-robot-policy-from-my-own-gpu.md)
2. **Your robot.** Fill in `observation_now_user`, `move_user` and `hold_user` in `quickstart_robot.py`, send the keys
   your model reads, and put one real observation in the sample.
3. **Its numbers.** Set `hz`, `action_chunk_valid_len` and `action_chunk_replan_at` to your robot's, and the same three
   at the top of the loop.
4. **Two machines.** The server already listens on every address; on the robot, give the GPU's address:

   ```bash
   seq serve                                             # on the GPU, in the policy's folder
   python quickstart_robot.py http://YOUR_GPU:8000       # on the robot
   ```
5. **A token.** Before a robot depends on it, start the server with one, `SEQ_SERVE_TOKEN=... seq serve`, and connect
   with `sequence_ai.connect(url, token=...)`. Open the port only to your robot as well.
6. **Measure the link.**
   [How do I measure the link between my robot and my GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md)
   tells you which components help on it.

## Where to go next

- [How do I serve a robot policy from my own GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-serve-a-robot-policy-from-my-own-gpu.md)
- [How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md)
- [How do I reduce the latency of LeRobot remote inference?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-reduce-the-latency-of-lerobot-remote-inference.md)
- [How do I get a GPU near my robot?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-get-a-gpu-near-my-robot.md)
- A step failed: [FAQ](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/faq.md)

# How do the components compare with openpi's remote inference and LeRobot's?

It does not replace either one. openpi and LeRobot each ship a complete way to run a policy on a remote GPU: a server
that loads the model, and a client on the robot that talks to it. The components here load no model. The network layer is a set
of components for the connection underneath, and you use it in one of three ways:

| You run | You keep | You add from `sequence_ai.network` |
|---|---|---|
| openpi | openpi's server and client, unchanged | on the robot, `openpi.keep(policy)`, and `image_tools` from `sequence_ai.network.openpi` for pictures as JPEG; on the GPU, `openpi.patch()` in its server script |
| LeRobot's remote inference | LeRobot's server and client, unchanged | one Zenoh setting, in a file: `lerobot.keep_alive_file(path)` |
| your own server | your model and your handler | `connect()` on the robot; `one_write`, `ping`, `compressed`, `tcp_link` on the server |

This page compares what each one does and does not do, from source inspection: openpi at commit `215abfb`
(2026-08-24), LeRobot 0.7.0, and this package's components. Results from tests are marked as such. No head-to-head measurement
against openpi or LeRobot has been made.

## Side by side

| | openpi | LeRobot 0.7.0 | These components |
|---|---|---|---|
| What it is | A policy server and a client for openpi's models | A policy server and a remote executor for LeRobot's policies | Components for the connection; no model loading |
| Starts with | `uv run scripts/serve_policy.py --env=...` and `WebsocketClientPolicy(host, port)` | `lerobot-policy-server` and `lerobot-rollout --inference.type=remote` | `serve(policy)` on the GPU, `sequence_ai.connect(url)` on the robot |
| Transport | WebSocket; the client opens one connection and reuses it | Zenoh, over TCP by default (`tcp/127.0.0.1:7447`) | The robot's stream: one WebSocket, kept open; options for WebSocket servers of your own |
| Message format | msgpack, numpy arrays as raw bytes | msgpack, arrays as raw bytes | msgpack, numpy arrays as raw bytes; reads openpi's array layout and msgpack-numpy's |
| Camera frames | Resized on the robot with `image_tools.resize_with_pad` | Sent raw, or as JPEG (`encoding`, `jpeg_quality`) | `frames.resize_image` (its `"pad"` is openpi's `resize_with_pad`), `frames.encode` for JPEG and `frames.decode` on the server, `openpi.image_tools` and `openpi.patch()` for openpi's own client and server; `sequence_ai.Video` as low-latency video, a picture not marked as a keyframe of its own (`pictures="exact"`: as it is) |
| Action chunks | `ActionChunkBroker` executes a chunk open-loop and requests the next when it is exhausted | Requests ahead of time, based on the turnaround it measured; aligns the new chunk with the one being executed; real-time chunking modes | None: `act()` returns what the policy returned |
| Robots on one server | Each connection's handler calls `policy.infer` itself; no batching across connections | One robot session; a second receives `busy` | Whatever your server does; `sequence_ai.engine` has `batcher`, `slack` and `replicas` |
| Timing it reports | `server_timing` in each response: the model's time in milliseconds | The turnaround of recent requests, kept by the client | p50, p95 and p99 of each act (`policy.stats()`); each client's RTT and retransmissions, from the server's kernel (`tcp_link`) |

## The connection between requests

This is the one area where the network layer adds to both, so it is described in full.

| | openpi | LeRobot 0.7.0 | These components |
|---|---|---|---|
| What is sent on an idle connection | The `websockets` library's own ping, every 20 seconds by default: neither openpi's `serve(...)` call nor its client's `connect(...)` passes another interval | Zenoh's keep-alive frames: on an idle link between two peers, one every 1.5 s or less often (seen with Zenoh 1.10.2) | A ping every 100 ms while idle: from the robot (`connect()`, `window.Warm`, `openpi.keep`) or from a WebSocket server (`ping`); for Zenoh, a setting that makes it a frame every 100 ms |
| Congestion control on the robot's socket | Not set, so the machine's default | Not set by LeRobot; Zenoh opens the sockets | BBR where Linux allows it (`window.socket_options()`, `window.keep(sock)`); not for Zenoh, which opens its own sockets |
| TCP keepalive | Not set by openpi's client, nor by the `websockets` library under it | Not checked | Set, where the machine accepts the options |
| Tells you what the machine does | No | No | `window.check()`: whether the kernel restarts a window after a pause; `wifi_power.check()`: Wi-Fi power saving |

Why the interval matters: on Linux, a connection that has sent nothing for longer than its retransmission timeout (at
least its round-trip time (RTT) plus 200 ms) has its congestion window restarted. A ping every 20 seconds, or a frame
every 1.5 seconds, is longer than that, so neither keeps a window through a robot's sub-second pauses. That is a
statement about the mechanism. Measure your own link with [`bench/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/tree/main/bench).

## Test coverage

| | Tested with |
|---|---|
| openpi | `openpi.keep()` on openpi-client 0.1.2's real `WebsocketClientPolicy`, against a stand-in server speaking openpi's protocol on one machine ([`examples/quickstart_openpi.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/quickstart_openpi.py), `tests/network/test_openpi.py`). On a real link: `openpi.keep()`, and a server that pings, on a WebSocket connection of the kind openpi holds, with a stand-in for its client ([Measurements](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md)). For the technical report: openpi's policy server (commit `215abfb`, `pi05_droid`, on an L4) and its own client in a closed loop over a home connection, with no network component of this package on the connection; and the same server and client with `openpi.keep()`, from a Linux virtual machine on a home connection ([the table](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md#openpikeep-with-openpis-own-server-and-client)); and the same server pinging and decoding the pictures as `openpi.patch()` makes it, with the client sending them as JPEG as `openpi.image_tools` does, from a Mac on a home connection ([the table](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md#pictures-as-jpeg-with-openpis-own-server-and-client)). `openpi.patch()`, the command and `image_tools` against a server module built as openpi's (`tests/network/test_openpi_server.py`) |
| LeRobot | The keep-alive file on Zenoh 1.10.2: two idle peers on one machine then sent a frame about every 100 ms each way (`tests/network/test_lerobot.py`). On a real link: two Zenoh peers, with and without the file ([Measurements](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md)) |
| The components alone | Every measurement in the [README's table](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/README.md#results), with the tool in [`bench/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/tree/main/bench) or the servers named there |

## Which should I use?

- **You serve an openpi model (π0, π0-FAST, π0.5).** Use openpi's server and client. Patch the server with
  `openpi.patch()` in its script and import `image_tools` from `sequence_ai.network.openpi` on the robot to send the pictures as JPEG, and
  add `openpi.keep(policy)` if the robot is on Linux and pauses between chunks:
  [How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md)
- **You serve a LeRobot policy.** Use LeRobot's remote inference. Add the Zenoh file on both sides:
  [How do I reduce the latency of LeRobot remote inference?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-reduce-the-latency-of-lerobot-remote-inference.md)
- **You have a model and no server yet, or your own server.** The network components are the transport:
  [How do I serve a robot policy from my own GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-serve-a-robot-policy-from-my-own-gpu.md) You then write, or
  take from another project, what openpi and LeRobot give you ready made: chunk playback on the robot, and the model's
  own input and output transforms.
- **Whichever you use,** [measure the link](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md) first. The tool
  needs neither project.

## Where each fact was read

openpi, commit `215abfb217dbac7d5f1273282331b9b1866c0479` (Apache-2.0):

- `src/openpi/serving/websocket_policy_server.py`: the `serve(...)` call and its arguments; the handler that unpacks
  an observation, calls `self._policy.infer(obs)` and sends the response with `server_timing`.
- `packages/openpi-client/src/openpi_client/websocket_client_policy.py`: the client's `connect(...)` call and its
  arguments; `infer`.
- `packages/openpi-client/src/openpi_client/action_chunk_broker.py`: `ActionChunkBroker`.
- `packages/openpi-client/src/openpi_client/msgpack_numpy.py`: the array layout.
- `packages/openpi-client/src/openpi_client/image_tools.py`: `resize_with_pad`.
- `docs/remote_inference.md`: the two commands and the client-side resize.

LeRobot 0.7.0 (Apache-2.0):

- `lerobot/inference/factory.py`, `RemoteInferenceConfig`: `endpoint`, `refill_seconds`, `chunk_merge`, `encoding`,
  `jpeg_quality`, `zenoh_config_path`.
- `lerobot/inference/execution.py`: the turnaround kept from recent requests and the refill threshold made from it.
- `lerobot/remote_inference/server.py` and `lerobot/scripts/lerobot_policy_server.py`: one robot session for a server.
- `lerobot/transport/zenoh.py`, `ZenohConfig`: `config_file`, and the keys `build()` sets over it.
- `lerobot/transport/protocol/codec.py`: msgpack, arrays as raw bytes, JPEG.
- `lerobot/scripts/lerobot_rollout.py`: `--inference.type=remote`.

The `websockets` library, version 17.4: `ping_interval: float | None = 20` in the signatures of its `serve` and
`connect`.

If a fact here is out of date or wrong, please open an issue at
<https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/issues>.

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/components.md

# What does each network component do?

Each component is one file that you can use independently. This page gives, for each: the lines to add, why it
exists, what was measured and on which link, and the output of its example. The examples were run on a Mac with
Python 3.12, so the components that read the Linux kernel return `None` or `False` there.

| Client side | Server side | Both sides | Combined |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`window`](#window-the-congestion-window-kept-through-the-pauses) | [`ping`](#ping-a-server-side-ping) | [`msgpack_io`](#msgpack_io) | [`connect`](#connect-the-robots-own-connection) |
| [`frames`](#frames-a-frame-resized-before-upload-and-decoded-on-the-server) | [`one_write`](#one_write-a-response-in-one-write) | [`latency_stats`](#latency_stats) | [`openpi`](#openpi-and-lerobot) |
| [`wifi_power`](#wifi_power-wi-fi-power-saving-detected) | [`tcp_link`](#tcp_link-each-clients-link-read-from-the-kernel) | | [`lerobot`](#openpi-and-lerobot) |
| | | | [`bench/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md) |

What a component saves depends on your link, and every number below is given with the link it was measured on. The
inference components (`sequence_ai.engine`) are described in the [README](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/README.md#inference-layer).

## Client side

### `window`: the congestion window, kept through the pauses

```python
from sequence_ai.network import window

transport_user = httpx.HTTPTransport(socket_options=window.socket_options())    # BBR and TCP keepalive, where it can
window.keep(sock_user)                                                          # or BBR on your own socket

warm_user = window.Warm(ping=lambda: client.get("/ping"))    # a ping while the connection is idle
warm_user.used()                                              # each time you send on it

window.check()                                           # warns once: what this machine does after a pause
```

**Why.** On Linux a connection that sends nothing for longer than its retransmission timeout has its congestion window
restarted, so the next upload takes one extra round trip. A robot that sends a request every half second incurs it on
every request.

**Measured.**

- **BBR.** A robot sending a request every 0.53 s with 24 KB of frames, on a round-trip time (RTT) of about 21 ms: 40 of
  40 requests took one more round trip without it (21.5 ms), and none with it (0.5 to 3.0 ms).
- **Where the pause cost nothing.** On RTTs of about 101 and 241 ms the same robot took no extra round trip
  with the default settings (0 or 1 of 40 requests), until the link lost packets (38 to 40 of 40 at 1% loss) or the size
  of the request varied.
- **A ping while idle.** On an RTT of 226 ms, 162 KB uploads 3 s apart took 303.6 ms to arrive without the
  pings, and under 1 ms with them.

A ping cannot keep a window that the pings do not fill; BBR, or `tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0`, keeps that one.

`window.check()` issues a warning once per process, with both ways to keep the window, and changes nothing on the
machine.
[Why does my robot's upload get slow after a pause?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/why-does-my-robots-upload-get-slow-after-a-pause.md) has the
full table.

`python examples/components/window.py` printed:

```text
socket options this machine accepts: [(65535, 8, 1), (6, 16, 20), (6, 257, 5), (6, 258, 3)]
restarts a window after a pause: False
BBR on your own socket: False; its congestion control: None
pings in 0.3 s of idle time: 5
```

### `frames`: a frame resized before upload, and decoded on the server

```python
from sequence_ai.network import frames

frame_user = frames.resize_image(camera_user.read(), 224, 224, mode="pad", filter="bilinear")
data_user = frames.encode(frame_user)            # a base64 JPEG
image_user = frames.decode(data_user)            # on the server: the HxWx3 uint8 array its policy reads
```

`"pad"` is openpi's `resize_with_pad`, byte for byte. The mode and the filter have no default and must be passed: a
policy sees what it was trained on. `frames.encode(frame)` gives a base64 JPEG for an input that carries its frames as
text, and `frames.image_size(data)` reads a frame's width and height from its header without Pillow. On the server,
`frames.decode(data)` turns that JPEG, or a PNG, back into the array, and returns an array it is given unchanged. It
opens no other format, since a picture comes over the network.

`python examples/components/frames.py` printed:

```text
pad: (224, 224, 3) with black rows at the top: True
stretch: (224, 224, 3)
encoded: 17,056 characters for 921,600 bytes; size from its header: (224, 224)
decoded: (224, 224, 3) uint8, 2.0 levels from the frame on average
```

### `wifi_power`: Wi-Fi power saving, detected

```python
from sequence_ai.network import wifi_power

wifi_power.check()    # the interface whose power saving is on, after warning how to disable it; else None
```

With power saving enabled, a Wi-Fi adapter sleeps between the access point's beacons, and a policy's response is
delayed until the adapter wakes. `check()` reads the machine's settings and changes nothing. Linux only.

`python examples/components/wifi_power.py` printed, on a Mac:

```text
Wi-Fi power saving is on: no (or this is not Linux, or not Wi-Fi)
```

### `connect`: the robot's own connection

```python
import sequence_ai

with sequence_ai.connect("http://your-gpu:8000") as policy_user:       # seq serve at that address
    policy_user.wait_until_ready()
    policy_user.observe({"image": sequence_ai.Video(frame_user), "state": state_user})
    actions_user = policy_user.act()["actions"]
    print(policy_user.stats()["latency_us"]["act_us"])                 # the acts' p50, p95 and p99
```

The same policy a deployed one's name gives, on the robot's stream: one WebSocket to the server, each observation sent
as it is made, and each act after them naming how many observations came before it. The server answers once those are
in, from the newest. What it does by default:

| | What it does | To change it |
|---|---|---|
| the stream | one WebSocket, kept open, with `window`'s socket options; a ping after each 100 ms of idle time, for 60 s after the last request | - |
| video | a `sequence_ai.Video` item goes as low-latency video (H.264), a keyframe every second and after anything lost | - |
| pictures | a picture you did not mark (H×W×3 uint8, each side 32 pixels or more) goes as a video keyframe of its own | `pictures="exact"` |
| large arrays | compressed where that saves upload time | - |
| lost and refused | an observation the server lost is sent again; one it refused is left out, and the video's next frame is a keyframe | - |
| lines | one line, by the default route | `lines=["eth0", "wwan0"]` |
| token | none | `token="..."` |

Your server is `seq serve`: it takes the robot's stream, and says so on every answer
(`X-Seq-Act-Formats`). `python -m sequence_ai.check http://your-gpu:8000` reaches it as the robot does and says what is
on.

**One connection, kept open.** This is one line in any client: create one `httpx.Client` and reuse it. Measured: a
new connection for each call took a median 305.9 ms; one reused connection, 121.0 ms. The handshake was 184.9 ms per
call. `connect()` keeps one.

## Server side

### `ping`: a server-side ping

```python
import websockets
from sequence_ai.network import ping

# websockets' own server, with a ping every 100 ms
async with ping.serve(handler_user, host_user, port_user) as server_user:
    await server_user.serve_forever()

# the same, as its options
async with websockets.serve(handler_user, host_user, port_user, **ping.websockets_options()):
    ...

uvicorn.run(app_user, **ping.uvicorn_options())                                         # the same, under uvicorn
```

A WebSocket library answers a ping with a pong by itself. A server that pings therefore makes the robot send a few
bytes each interval, and the robot's kernel never counts the connection idle. Nothing changes on the robot.

**Measured.** Between machines of one cloud provider, on RTTs of 11.7 and 69.2 ms, an upload after 500 ms of silence
took 3.0 round trips; with the server pinging every 100 ms it took 1.1 (100 KB and 500 KB) and 1.25 (1 MB).

A server that answers one HTTP request with one response cannot send anything unsolicited. There the ping comes from the
robot: `window.Warm`, which `connect()` applies to its connection. [How do I keep a WebSocket policy server's connection
warm?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-keep-a-websocket-policy-servers-connection-warm.md) has the rest.

`python examples/components/ping.py` printed:

```text
response: observation
the server measured the connection's RTT from its pings: 0.17 ms
```

### `one_write`: a response in one write

```python
import uvicorn
from sequence_ai.network.one_write import WholeResponse, one_write_http

uvicorn.run(WholeResponse(app_user), http=one_write_http())
```

`app_user` is any ASGI app: FastAPI's and Starlette's too.

uvicorn writes a response in pieces. A tunnel or proxy in front of the server can delay every piece after the first
until the client has acknowledged the first, so each request takes one more round trip than necessary.

**Measured.** Behind such a tunnel, with a TCP connect of p50 89.5 ms: headers then body, GET p50 189.7 ms; the same
response in one write, 106.7 ms.

`python examples/components/one_write.py` printed `response: b'ok'`.

### `tcp_link`: each client's link, read from the kernel

```python
from sequence_ai.network import tcp_link

tcp_link.read(sock_user)             # any connected socket
tcp_link.of(scope_user["client"])    # in an ASGI app served with one_write_http(): this request's own connection
```

Each returns `rtt_ms`, `rttvar_ms`, `retrans`, `total_retrans`, `cwnd` and, where the kernel provides it,
`delivery_kbps`; or `None` where the kernel provides none, as on macOS. A robot's own OS may not expose these to
the program that runs on it, and the server reads every robot the same way.

`python examples/components/tcp_link.py` printed, on a Mac:

```text
this connection, as the server's kernel reports it: None
```

## Both sides

### `msgpack_io`

```python
from sequence_ai.network import msgpack_io

body_user = msgpack_io.pack({"image": frame_user, "state": joints_user})
observation_user = msgpack_io.unpack(body_user)
```

Bytes are sent as bytes and numpy arrays as their raw data, whereas JSON carries bytes as base64, a third larger on the
wire. It is plain Python, so neither side installs a msgpack package. It writes arrays as msgpack-numpy does and reads
openpi's layout as well. An object array is rejected: decoding one would run code chosen by the sender.

`python examples/components/msgpack_io.py` printed:

```text
150,670 bytes for an image of 150,528; content type application/x-seq-msgpack
arrays returned as arrays: (224, 224, 3) float32
```

### `latency_stats`

```python
from sequence_ai.network.latency_stats import LatencyStats, now_us

stats_user = LatencyStats(latencies=["request_us"])
sent_user = now_us(); ...; stats_user.since("request_us", sent_user)
stats_user.snapshot()["latency_us"]["request_us"]    # n, mean, max, p50, p95, p99
```

A percentile is `None` until its window contains enough samples for it: the p99 of 20 samples is only the largest of the
20. So p50 needs 2 samples, p95 needs 20 and p99 needs 100.

`python examples/components/latency_stats.py` printed:

```text
200 requests: p50 248 ms, p95 281 ms, p99 290 ms
```

## openpi and LeRobot

**openpi.** Keep openpi's client and server. On the GPU, `openpi.patch()` in openpi's server script, before it makes
the server: it then pings each robot every 100 ms while no inference runs, and hands its policy each picture sent as
JPEG as the array it reads. openpi's server runs its policy on its event loop, which sends and answers no ping while an
inference runs, so it waits for each pong as long as that takes. On the robot, import `image_tools` from here, so its
pictures go as JPEG, and add the client-side components to the connection the client holds.

```python
from sequence_ai.network import openpi

openpi.patch()                                        # the GPU: in openpi's scripts/serve_policy.py, before the server
```

```python
from sequence_ai.network import openpi
from sequence_ai.network.openpi import image_tools     # in place of openpi_client's: pictures go as JPEG

policy_user = openpi.connect(host_user, port_user)    # openpi_client's own client, once its server answers
kept_user = openpi.keep(policy_user)  # BBR and TCP keepalive on its socket; a WebSocket ping while it is idle
observation_user["observation/image"] = image_tools.resize_with_pad(frame_user, 224, 224)
action_user = policy_user.infer(observation_user)     # as before
```

`keep()` is verified against openpi-client 0.1.2 on a local connection, and the server side and `image_tools` against
a server module built as openpi's `websocket_policy_server.py` is. Measured on a WebSocket connection of the kind
openpi's client holds, between two cloud machines: a 100 KB upload 0.53 s after each response took two to three round
trips without `keep()` and one with it ([Measurements](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md)). With openpi's own server and client, `keep()`
was measured in one closed-loop run ([the table](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md#openpikeep-with-openpis-own-server-and-client)), and
the pictures as JPEG with the server's pings in another
([the table](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md#pictures-as-jpeg-with-openpis-own-server-and-client)).
[How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md)

**LeRobot.** LeRobot 0.7.0's remote inference talks over Zenoh, which sends a frame on an idle link only every few
seconds. One setting makes it every 100 ms:

```python
from sequence_ai.network import lerobot

path_user = lerobot.keep_alive_file("zenoh-keep-alive.json5")
```

Give the file to both sides: the policy server reads it from `zenoh.config_file`, and the robot's remote inference
from `zenoh_config_path`.

Checked: Zenoh 1.10.2 takes the setting, and two idle peers on one machine then sent a frame every 102 ms each way.
Measured between two Zenoh peers on two cloud machines: a 100 KB request 0.53 s after each response took two to three
round trips without the file and one with it ([Measurements](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md)).
[How do I reduce the latency of LeRobot remote inference?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-reduce-the-latency-of-lerobot-remote-inference.md)

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/faq.md

# FAQ: errors you may see, and what to do next

Each entry starts with what to do. The error text under it is the code's output when the error was reproduced
(macOS on Apple silicon, Python 3.12, sequence-ai 0.62.0, httpx 0.28, uvicorn 0.54), unless the entry states
otherwise.

Network layer (`sequence_ai.network`):

- [Installing](#installing)
- [Connecting](#connecting)
- [Sending and reading](#sending-and-reading)
- [With openpi and LeRobot](#with-openpi-and-lerobot)
- [On the server](#on-the-server)
- [What a component reports about your machine](#what-a-component-reports-about-your-machine)
- [A network component made nothing faster](#a-network-component-made-nothing-faster)

Inference layer (`sequence_ai.engine`):

- [`optimize`](#optimize)
- [`batcher`](#batcher)
- [`replicas`](#replicas)
- [`slack`](#slack)

[General](#general)

## Installing

### `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy'` or `'uvicorn'`

The quickstart's two files import numpy, and its server runs under uvicorn. Both are dependencies of `sequence-ai`, so
`pip install sequence-ai` installs them. The error appears where the files were copied into a project that has neither:
`pip install numpy uvicorn`.

```text
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy'
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'uvicorn'
```

numpy is optional for the components themselves. Without it, `connect()` and `msgpack_io` carry plain values, and an
array the server sent comes back as nested lists:

```text
{'state': [0.0, 1.0], 'prompt': 'pick'}
```

### `ImportError: resizing a frame needs Pillow, which is not installed here`

Pillow is a dependency of `sequence-ai`. The error appears where `frames.py` was copied into a project that has no
Pillow: `pip install pillow`. `frames.resize_image`, `frames.encode` and `frames.decode` use Pillow, and
`openpi.image_tools` and `openpi.patch()` through them; no other component does.

```text
ImportError: resizing a frame needs Pillow, which is not installed here: pip install pillow
ImportError: encoding an array or PIL image needs Pillow, and it is missing or broken here: pip install pillow. Pass an already-encoded base64 str or bytes to avoid it.
```

The first line is what `frames.resize_image` raises, the second what `frames.encode` raises.

### What do I install?

| You use | Install |
|---|---|
| `connect()` on the robot, `frames`, `window`, `ping`, `tcp_link`, `one_write` under uvicorn, `wifi_power`, `msgpack_io`, `latency_stats`, `lerobot`, every inference component, numpy arrays in observations or responses | `sequence-ai`, nothing more |
| `seq serve`, and the quick start's server | `sequence-ai`, on Python 3.10 or later |
| `sequence_ai.Video`, `Depth` and `Tactile`, and pictures sent as video keyframes, `connect()`'s default | `sequence-ai`, on Python 3.10 or later; on 3.9, pictures go as they are |
| `bench/`, the measuring tool | a checkout of the repository; it is standard library only |

Python 3.9 or later on the robot; 3.10 or later for `seq serve` and for video.

## Connecting

### `Unavailable: ... had no answer from http://...:8000 (nothing listens there, or this machine's network does not reach it)`

`wait_until_ready()` reached nothing at that address before its bound. Check, in this order:

1. The server is running, and its log shows the port you gave `connect()`.
2. The server listens on an address the robot can reach. `127.0.0.1` is reachable from the same machine only.
   `seq serve` listens on every address unless it is given `--host`.
3. The URL starts with `http://`, has the port, and its host name resolves: `connect("http://YOUR_GPU:8000")`. A
   misspelled name gives the same line.
4. The GPU's firewall lets the robot's address in on that port: a closed one drops the robot's packets, and nothing
   answers.

```text
sequence_ai.errors.Unavailable: 127.0.0.1-8000 had no answer from http://127.0.0.1:8000 (nothing listens there, or this machine's network does not reach it) after 3s (wait_until_ready timeout_s)
```

Without `wait_until_ready()`, the first act meets the same thing as it opens the robot's stream:

```text
sequence_ai.errors.Unavailable: worker unreachable after 5 reconnect attempts: the stream to the worker did not open: the worker could not be reached (1 try in 0.0 s, the last in its TCP connect)
```

## Sending and reading

### `AuthError: the server at ... refused this robot's ping (401)`

The server was started with a token, and the robot sent none or another. Connect with the server's token:
`sequence_ai.connect(url, token="...")`, the one `seq serve` was given with `--token` or as `SEQ_SERVE_TOKEN` on the
GPU. `wait_until_ready()` raises it at once: asking again changes nothing.

```text
sequence_ai.errors.AuthError: the server at http://127.0.0.1:8000 refused this robot's ping (401) (hint: it asks for its token: connect(url, token=...))
```

### `PolicyError: the policy raised ...`

The policy raised on the observation the act was answered from. The server's log has the traceback, and the server
goes on answering the next acts.

```text
sequence_ai.errors.PolicyError: the policy raised KeyError: 'camera'
```

### `PolicyError: the policy's answer cannot go back as msgpack: ...`

The policy returned something msgpack cannot carry. Return JSON-like values, bytes and numpy arrays; torch tensors and
JAX arrays are turned into numpy arrays for you.

```text
sequence_ai.errors.PolicyError: the policy's answer cannot go back as msgpack: object cannot be sent as msgpack (JSON values, bytes and numpy arrays can)
```

### `InvalidRequest: observe(): this observation cannot be sent - ...`

The observation contains something msgpack cannot carry, and nothing was sent. Send JSON-like values, bytes and numpy
arrays: convert a set to a list, and an object to a dict of its fields. An array of Python objects (dtype object) is
refused on purpose: reading one back would run code the sender chose.

```text
sequence_ai.errors.InvalidRequest: observe(): this observation cannot be sent - set cannot be sent as msgpack (JSON values, bytes and numpy arrays can)
sequence_ai.errors.InvalidRequest: observe(): this observation cannot be sent - a numpy array of dtype object is not carried: only plain numeric, bool and string dtypes are
```

## With openpi and LeRobot

### `TypeError: this client keeps no WebSocket connection at _ws`

`openpi.keep()` takes openpi's own `WebsocketClientPolicy`, which holds its connection at `_ws`. Pass that object,
and not a wrapper around it such as an `ActionChunkBroker`.

```text
TypeError: this client keeps no WebSocket connection at `_ws` (openpi_client's WebsocketClientPolicy does): nothing to keep warm
```

### `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'openpi_client'`

Install openpi's client from openpi's repository (`packages/openpi-client`, `pip install -e .`).
`sequence_ai.network.openpi` adds to that client and does not replace it.

```text
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'openpi_client'
```

### `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'typing_extensions'` on importing `openpi_client`

`pip install typing_extensions`. openpi-client 0.1.0 imports it without listing it as a dependency, so a new
environment that contains only openpi's client may lack it; inside openpi's own environment it is already there.

```text
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'typing_extensions'
```

### My openpi client prints nothing and never returns

It is waiting for the server. While the connection is refused, openpi's client retries it every 5 seconds, and logs
`Waiting for server at ...` and `Still waiting for server...` at INFO level, which is hidden unless logging is set
up. So the server is not up yet, or the port is wrong. This is read from openpi's source
(`websocket_client_policy.py`); it was not made to happen here.

### `BBR on its socket: False`

Expected anywhere but Linux, and on Linux until the BBR module is loaded: `sudo modprobe tcp_bbr`. The keepalive
options and the ping while idle are on either way. On this Mac:

```text
BBR on its socket: False; TCP keepalive options accepted: 4
```

### Does the LeRobot setting need to be applied on both sides?

Yes, each side sends its own keep-alive frames. In LeRobot 0.7.0 the policy server reads it from `zenoh.config_file`
and the robot's remote inference from `zenoh_config_path`. Both names are from LeRobot's source; the file has not been
tested with LeRobot's own client and server. See
[How do I reduce the latency of LeRobot remote inference?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-reduce-the-latency-of-lerobot-remote-inference.md)

## On the server

### `OSError: [Errno 48] port 8000 is taken: a server already answers at 127.0.0.1:8000 on this machine`

Another program has the port, often an earlier `seq serve` still running: `lsof -nP -iTCP:8000 -sTCP:LISTEN` names it.
Stop it, or give the server and the robot another port:

```bash
seq serve --port 8001                                    # in the policy's folder
python quickstart_robot.py http://127.0.0.1:8001
```

`seq serve` (sequence-ai 0.64.1) prints, last:

```text
OSError: [Errno 48] port 8000 is taken: a server already answers at 127.0.0.1:8000 on this machine (an earlier serve() still running?); stop it, or pass another port
```

A uvicorn server of your own prints:

```text
ERROR:    [Errno 48] error while attempting to bind on address ('127.0.0.1', 8000): [errno 48] address already in use
```

### `ERROR: the policy failed on the example (KeyError: 'camera'): stopping`

`seq serve` ran the policy on its sample's first observation before saying it is ready, and the policy raised: the
server stops, and the traceback it raises is the policy's own. Give `@seq.sample` the keys and shapes your robot sends,
or fix the policy. With a policy that reads a key its sample does not have (sequence-ai 0.64.1):

```text
ERROR:    the policy failed on the example (KeyError: 'camera'): stopping
INFO:     Shutting down
...
KeyError: 'camera'
```

### Can the server ping instead, so the robot's code does not change?

Only over a WebSocket. A server that answers one HTTP request with one response cannot send anything unsolicited. See
[How do I keep a WebSocket policy server's connection warm?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-keep-a-websocket-policy-servers-connection-warm.md)

## What a component reports about your machine

### `UserWarning: this machine restarts a connection's send window after each pause`

Do one of the two things it names, once, on the robot. Both need root. `connect(url, check=False)` disables the
warning without changing anything. The text below is the package's own, printed on a Mac with the Linux state
simulated; it is issued on Linux only.

```text
UserWarning: this machine restarts a connection's send window after each pause (net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle is 1), so an upload of 0.3 MB sent after one takes several round trips. `sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0` keeps the window through pauses (a line in /etc/sysctl.d/ keeps it after a reboot), as does loading BBR (`sudo modprobe tcp_bbr`), which window.socket_options() then sets on your connections
```

[Why does my robot's upload get slow after a pause?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/why-does-my-robots-upload-get-slow-after-a-pause.md) explains it.

### `Wi-Fi power saving is on for wlan0`

Run the command it gives on the robot. The text is the package's own, printed here for an interface named `wlan0`; it
is issued on Linux only, when the robot's default route is a Wi-Fi interface with power saving enabled.

```text
Wi-Fi power saving is on for wlan0, so its adapter can delay this robot's packets while it sleeps; `sudo iw dev wlan0 set power_save off` disables it until the next reboot, and `wifi.powersave = 2` under [connection] in a file in /etc/NetworkManager/conf.d/ keeps it disabled
```

### `window.keep(sock)` returns `False`, `tcp_link.read(sock)` and `wifi_power.check()` return `None`

Expected off Linux: those three read or set things only the Linux kernel has. Nothing fails, and the rest works. On
this Mac:

```text
window.keep(sock): False | window.congestion_of(sock): None
window.restarts_after_idle(): False | window.check(): False
tcp_link.read(sock): None
wifi_power.check(): None
```

On Linux, `window.keep(sock)` is `False` until the kernel's BBR module is loaded (`sudo modprobe tcp_bbr`).

## A network component made nothing faster

What a network component saves depends on the link:

- On round-trip times (RTTs) of about 101 and 241 ms, a robot sending a request every 0.53 s took no extra round trip
  after its pauses with the default settings, so there was nothing for BBR or a ping to save.
- On loopback, or between two machines on one switch, a round trip costs almost nothing, so saving one saves almost
  nothing.

The README has the [results](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/README.md#results).
[Measure your own link](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md) before and after.

## `optimize`

`seq serve` tries the speed-ups during the warm-up and prints one line for each switch it tries. A switch that stays
off says why; the model keeps running as it was.

### `optimize: nothing turned on - this machine has no CUDA GPU`

The switches that keep the outputs exactly the same need a CUDA GPU that torch, or JAX, can use. That is the expected
line on a laptop. On a machine that has a GPU, check `torch.cuda.is_available()`: a CPU-only build of torch prints the
same line.

### `optimize: nothing turned on - no observation to check the outputs on: give examples=, or the policy a @seq.sample method`

The checks run the policy on the observations of its `@seq.sample` episode. Give it one, preferably of 32 or more of
your robot's own observations.

### `optimize: cuda_graphs off - no module is called more than once a run with the same shapes`

A module called once per run has no launches to save across calls, so no module was graphed. `whole_graph` can still
cover the run's whole call; its line says whether it did.

### `optimize: cuda_graphs off - its outputs differed from eager mode's on run ...`

A graph replayed an output that is not eager mode's byte for byte, so it was taken out and the model runs as it did.
The check is working as intended.

### `optimize: whole_graph off - the policy raised with it on: ...`

The policy's own code refused its call once it was replayed from a graph, with its own error after the colon: code
that reads a value back from the GPU in the middle of a run cannot be captured whole. The modules `cuda_graphs` graphs
are unaffected.

### `optimize: cuda_graphs off - 1% faster (act ... ms), under the 10% it needs`

A switch stays on only when acts are at least 10% faster with it, so it was taken out and the model runs as it did. A
switch that changes the outputs is timed as it will run, with `cuda_graphs` on in both turns, and the times on its
line say `with cuda_graphs on in both`.

### `ValueError: torch_compile changes the policy's outputs: give tolerance=...`

`torch_compile`, `fused_kernels`, `tensorrt` and `precision` change the outputs, so each runs only with the difference
you accept: `seq serve --tolerance 1e-3`, or `--tolerance max_abs=0.02,cosine=0.999`.

### Every switch stayed off: no faster

In order of likelihood:

1. **The model was not launch-bound.** A model whose GPU is already busy nearly all the time has no launch overhead
   to remove: π0.5 under JAX was 98% GPU-busy.
2. **Every call has a new shape.** Each new shape is captured once; a run of new shapes is a run of captures.
3. **The sample episode was not the robot's.** Make the `@seq.sample` episode's observations as your robot sends them,
   so the shapes checked are the shapes served.

[How do I make a policy faster without changing its outputs, and what does each switch
change?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-make-a-policy-faster-without-changing-its-outputs.md)

## `batcher`

### `ValueError: sizes [2, 4] must include 1: a call that waits alone is a batch of 1, and a batch in which the model raised is re-run call by call`

Include 1 in the sizes: `Batcher(run, sizes=[1, 2, 4])`. A call that arrives alone must be dispatched as a batch of
one.

### `ValueError: the model returned 3 outputs for a batch of 4`

Your function must return one output for each input, in order. It is given a list and returns a list of the same
length.

### My batches are all of size 1

Calls are batched only while they wait. With an idle model and `wait_ms=0`, each call is dispatched as soon as it
arrives. Raise `wait_ms` slightly (the examples use 2 ms), or expect batches only when the model is busy.

## `replicas`

### `TypeError: load must be a function a new process can import: defined at a module's top level, not a lambda and not a function inside another`

Each replica starts in its own process and imports `load_user` by name. Move it to the top of a module:

```python
def load_user():                       # at the top of a module, not inside main() and not a lambda
    model_user = build_model_user()
    return model_user.infer            # what one call runs
```

### `ReplicaStartFailed: the model's load raised: ...`

Your `load_user` raised in the replica's process; the text after the colon is its error, and the exception's `traceback`
