Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-serve-my-own-model.md

# How do I serve my own model?

Write a class around it: load the model in `__init__` the way its own README does, call it in `@seq.infer`, and serve
the class with `seq serve`. Nothing in the model changes. Below is Octo (`octo-base-1.5`, under JAX), written from Octo's
README alone.

## On the GPU

Install Octo as its README says, and `pip install sequence-ai` beside it. Then, as `policy.py` in a folder of its own:

```python
import jax
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image
from octo.model.octo_model import OctoModel

import seq


@seq.policy(hz=5, action_chunk_valid_len=4, action_chunk_replan_at=2)    # your robot's numbers: Octo returns 4 steps
class Octo_user:
    def __init__(self):
        self.model_user = OctoModel.load_pretrained("hf://rail-berkeley/octo-base-1.5")   # as Octo's README loads it
        self.calls_user = 0

    @seq.sample
    def sample_user(self):
        observation_user = {"image": np.zeros((224, 224, 3), np.uint8),
                            "prompt": "pick up the black block and put it in the box"}
        return [("observe", observation_user), ("act",)] * 3

    @seq.infer
    def infer_user(self, observation_user):
        self.calls_user += 1
        image_user = np.asarray(Image.fromarray(observation_user["image"]).resize((256, 256)))   # this model's size
        task_user = self.model_user.create_tasks(texts=[observation_user["prompt"]])
        actions_user = self.model_user.sample_actions(
            {"image_primary": image_user[None, None], "timestep_pad_mask": np.array([[True]])},  # a history of one
            task_user, rng=jax.random.PRNGKey(self.calls_user))
        return {"actions": np.asarray(actions_user, dtype=np.float32)[0]}                 # a chunk: 4 steps of 7
```

```bash
seq serve                    # in the policy's folder
```

`@seq.sample` is played before the server answers its first robot, so JAX compiles the model then, not on a robot's
first request. The observation is the one Octo's README names: `image_primary` with a history of one, and
`timestep_pad_mask`. The actions are what `sample_actions` returns, their first dimension time.

## On the robot

```python
import sequence_ai

policy_user = sequence_ai.connect("http://YOUR_GPU:8000")
policy_user.wait_until_ready()
prompt_user = "pick up the black block and put it in the box"
policy_user.observe({"image": frame_user, "prompt": prompt_user})  # frame_user: the camera's
chunk_user = policy_user.act()["actions"]
```

`chunk_user` is the 4 x 7 chunk the policy returned. The picture goes as JPEG and comes back to the policy as the
array it reads, as [What is on by default](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/what-is-on-by-default.md) says.

## Return an action chunk

The robot plays a chunk while it asks for the next one, so a round trip can pass while the arm moves. A policy that
returns one step at a time leaves the arm waiting for each step:
[How do I serve a robot policy from my own GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-serve-a-robot-policy-from-my-own-gpu.md#your-model-in-a-class)

## A PyTorch model

The same class, with the model's PyTorch call in `@seq.infer`:
[How do I serve a robot policy from my own GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-serve-a-robot-policy-from-my-own-gpu.md#your-model-in-a-class)
has a PyTorch module, [How do I make a PyTorch robot policy faster without changing its
outputs?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-make-a-pytorch-robot-policy-faster-without-changing-its-outputs.md) has GR00T, and [How do I
reduce the latency of LeRobot remote inference?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-reduce-the-latency-of-lerobot-remote-inference.md) has
LeRobot's policies.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-use-an-llm-with-my-own-openrouter-key.md

# How do I use an LLM with my own OpenRouter key?

Pass `server="openrouter"` to `sequence_ai.chat()`, with your own OpenRouter key in `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`. The call
goes from your machine to that server and returns the same result as any chat: `.content`, `.tool_calls`,
`.reasoning`, `.usage`.

```bash
pip install sequence-ai
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...      # your own OpenRouter key
```

```python
import sequence_ai

result_user = sequence_ai.chat(
    "qwen/qwen3-next-80b-a3b-instruct",                # the model's name on that server
    [{"role": "user", "content": "List the steps to put the red block in the bowl."}],
    server="openrouter",
)
print(result_user.content)
```

`api_key=` passes the key in the call instead of the environment.

## An agent that calls tools

`Conversation` keeps the history, and sends every turn to its `server`:

```python
import json

import sequence_ai

tools_user = [{"type": "function", "function": {
    "name": "move_above", "description": "Move the gripper above an object.",
    "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"object": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["object"]}}}]


def run_tool_user(call_user):
    arguments_user = json.loads(call_user["function"]["arguments"])
    return {"above": arguments_user["object"]}         # your robot's code here


conversation_user = sequence_ai.Conversation("qwen/qwen3-next-80b-a3b-instruct", server="openrouter",
                                             system="You plan robot tasks.", tools=tools_user)
reply_user = conversation_user.send("Put the red block in the bowl.")
while reply_user.tool_calls:
    for call_user in reply_user.tool_calls:
        conversation_user.tool_result(call_user["id"], run_tool_user(call_user))
    reply_user = conversation_user.send()
print(reply_user.content)
```

## Streaming

`stream=True` yields the text as it is generated; `.result` is the whole reply once the loop ends:

```python
import sequence_ai

stream_user = sequence_ai.chat("qwen/qwen3-next-80b-a3b-instruct", [{"role": "user", "content": "Describe the scene."}],
                               server="openrouter", stream=True)
for piece_user in stream_user:
    print(piece_user, end="", flush=True)
print(stream_user.result.usage)
```

## A server of your own

A server of your own with the OpenAI chat completions API works the same way: pass its address as `server`.

```python
import sequence_ai

result_user = sequence_ai.chat("my-model", [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}],
                               server="http://localhost:8000/v1")      # the model as your server names it
```

`api_key` is sent to an address only when you pass it.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-use-the-inference-components-with-openpi-lerobot-or-gr00t.md

# How do I use the inference components with openpi, LeRobot or GR00T?

Keep the model and the server you have, and add the component that fits where your model spends its time. Which
component applies depends on the framework the policy runs in, not on its name:

| Your policy | `optimize` | `batcher` and `slack` | `replicas` |
|---|---|---|---|
| A PyTorch policy with a denoising loop: GR00T, LeRobot's diffusion and flow policies, or your own | Applies: CUDA graphs of what repeats, measured on GR00T N1.7 | Apply where your model takes a batch | One replica per GPU |
| openpi's models under JAX (π0, π0.5) | Tried when you ask, `cuda_graphs=True, whole_graph=True`: XLA already compiles each jitted function whole, and π0.5 keeps its GPU 98% busy | Apply. Measured on π0.5's batched call, and `slack` in a test server around it | One replica per GPU |

What follows is where each component goes and what was measured on the models themselves.

## GR00T, and other PyTorch policies: a faster forward pass

```python
import sequence_ai

# infer_user(observation) -> its output: your policy's call, as your code makes it
fast_user = sequence_ai.engine.optimize(infer_user, examples_user)    # 32 or more of your robot's observations
print(fast_user.report["on"])                                          # for example ["cuda_graphs", "whole_graph"]
```

`serve(infer_user, ...)` runs the same during its warm-up. Measured: GR00T N1.7 on an L4, its DiT captured, 224 ms to
146 ms per run, with exactly the same outputs on inputs it was not captured on. The report says which modules were
graphed and why any switch stayed off, and
[`examples/check_on_a_gpu.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/check_on_a_gpu.py) compares every output with eager mode's on your GPU. [How do I make a PyTorch robot policy faster without changing its
outputs?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-make-a-pytorch-robot-policy-faster-without-changing-its-outputs.md)

## openpi and LeRobot: more than one robot on a GPU

openpi's policy server calls the model once for each request, with no batching across connections, and LeRobot 0.7's
policy server holds one robot session (both verified in their source code:
[the comparison page](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/comparison.md)). To
serve several robots in one forward pass, the requests must reach the model as a batch. With `seq serve` that is one
decorator, `@seq.concurrent`, and for an openpi policy `batched(policy)` of
[`examples/serve_openpi_batched.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/serve_openpi_batched.py) is the batched call:

```python
from openpi.policies import droid_policy

import seq
from serve_openpi_batched import batched     # the example's file, copied beside your policy


@seq.policy(hz=15, action_chunk_valid_len=15, action_chunk_replan_at=8)
class Pi05DroidBatched_user:
    def __init__(self):
        self.batched_user = batched(load_policy_user())            # openpi's infer() for a list of observations

    @seq.sample
    def sample_user(self):
        return [("observe", droid_policy.make_droid_example()), ("act",)] * 3

    @seq.concurrent(sizes=[1, 2, 4], collate=False)
    @seq.infer
    def infer_user(self, observations_user):                        # the acts that run together, as a list
        return self.batched_user(observations_user)                 # one sampling call, an answer for each
```

`load_policy_user()` makes openpi's trained policy from its downloaded checkpoint, as
[How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md#or-serve-the-policy-as-a-class)
shows.

In a server of your own, a handler around the model's batched call does the same:

```python
from sequence_ai.engine.batcher import Batcher

# infer_a_batch_user(observations: list) -> list
batcher_user = Batcher(infer_a_batch_user, sizes=[1, 2, 4], wait_ms=2.0)
output_user = await batcher_user(observation_user)  # in each connection's handler
```

`infer_a_batch_user` stacks the observations, calls the model once, and splits the output. For an openpi policy that is
each observation through the policy's input transform, the results stacked, one call of the model's `sample_actions`,
and each row through the output transform: the example's `batched(policy)` does exactly that. Under JAX each batch size
compiles on its first call: a policy compiled on its first inference can take tens of seconds, so `@seq.sample` runs it
before the server says it is ready.

A server that holds a batch by each robot's slack runs its own loop with `slack` in place of `Batcher`:
[How many robots can one GPU serve?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md#measured) has what one GPU answered in time.

## Any of them: the model off the server's event loop

```python
from sequence_ai.engine.replicas import ReplicaPool

pool_user = ReplicaPool(load_user, replicas=1)                     # load_user() builds the policy in its own process
output_user = await pool_user.run(observation_user)
```

Run one replica per GPU: one copy of the model answers all its robots in one pass.

## The connection to the robot

The inference components run on the server. For the link between the robot and the GPU, with openpi's own client or
LeRobot's remote inference kept as they are, the network layer adds one line on openpi's client ([How do I run π0
(openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md)) or one Zenoh setting for LeRobot ([How do I
reduce the latency of LeRobot remote inference?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-reduce-the-latency-of-lerobot-remote-inference.md)).

## When it applies

- `optimize`'s graphs apply to PyTorch models; a JAX model compiles its own kernels, and gets XLA's command buffers.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md

# How many robots can one GPU serve?

As many as it can answer in time. A policy that responds with a chunk of actions leaves its robot some steps still to
execute when it requests the next chunk: that buffer, less the robot's round-trip time (RTT) and a margin, is how long a
batch may take. `slack` computes, on a clock, how many robots a replica of the model answers in time from each robot's
buffer and the model's batch times, and names the robots it cannot serve; `batcher` then sends their requests as
batches.

```python
from sequence_ai.engine import slack

table_user = slack.measure(forward_of_user, sizes=[1, 2, 4])  # forward_of_user(n): one forward pass of n requests
play_user = slack.playback(hz=20, valid_len=15, replan_at=8)  # 15 valid steps, the next requested at the 8th
seating_user = slack.Seating(table_user, play_user["buffer_s"] * 1000, sizes=[1, 2, 4],
                             cycle_ms=(play_user["play_s"] - play_user["buffer_s"]) * 1000)
seats_user, over_user = seating_user.seat([("near", 30.0), ("far", 200.0)])     # (robot, its RTT in ms)
```

With batches of 1, 2 and 4 that take 80, 110 and 130 ms, this gives `(4, ["far"])`: the replica has capacity for
four robots, and the one 200 ms away is the one to move to another replica. `python examples/components/slack.py`
prints that case with no model and no GPU.

## The limits

- **Latency.** A robot fits the largest listed batch size whose batch time, plus the robot's own RTT and 50 ms, is
  within the buffer. A robot further away has less of its buffer left for the server, so it fits a smaller batch.
- **The batches a request arrives behind.** A replica runs one batch at a time, and robots send on their own clocks:
  a request that arrives as another batch runs waits for it, and is in time or not depending on how far apart the
  robots' requests fall. No formula has that, so `slack` runs 2, 3 and more robots on a simulated clock, as its
  server loop would serve them, from starts spread evenly over every way their requests can fall in a cycle (64 for
  two robots, 128 for more). A number of robots is within capacity when at least 95% of their responses are back
  before their robot's buffer runs out, each start counting the same.
- **Load.** In each of those starts the robots' batches may fill at most 0.9 of a cycle, the time between one robot's
  requests. Past that, responses queue behind each other however the requests are batched.

The first number of robots that fails ends the count: robots are admitted one at a time, so a replica reaches a
number of robots through every smaller one. In the example above a batch of four fits the buffer of a robot 100 ms
away (130 + 100 + 50 ms, within 350), and the capacity is four: on the clock four such robots have every response in
time, and their batches fill no more than 0.68 of a cycle.

Each robot is evaluated by its own RTT. When every robot was evaluated by the furthest robot's RTT, one far robot
lowered the batch size, and with it the capacity, of every near robot on the same replica.

## Using it

The policy says its buffer: `@seq.policy(hz=15, action_chunk_valid_len=8, action_chunk_replan_at=5)` is 15 steps a
second, the first 8 of each chunk played, the next asked for at the 5th. With `seq serve`, batching is one decorator:
`@seq.concurrent(sizes=[1, 2, 4, 8])` on the `@seq.infer` method hands it the observations waiting, stacked, through the
`Batcher` below, and each robot gets its own row back ([How do I serve a robot policy from my own
GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-serve-a-robot-policy-from-my-own-gpu.md#your-model-in-a-class)). In a server of your own:

```python
from sequence_ai.engine.batcher import Batcher

# model_on_a_list_user(inputs: list) -> list
batcher_user = Batcher(model_on_a_list_user, sizes=[1, 2, 4, 8], wait_ms=2.0)
output_user = await batcher_user(observation_user)  # in each request's handler
```

- A batch is dispatched as soon as it is full, or `wait_ms` after its first call arrived while the model is free.
- While the model is busy, waiting calls keep accumulating and are dispatched together as soon as it is free.
- Only the sizes you list are sent: with sizes `[1, 2, 4]`, three waiting calls are dispatched as a batch of 2, then
  a batch of 1.
- A batch in which the model raised is re-run call by call, so only the call that fails by itself fails.

`Batcher` waits one fixed time for every caller and has no notion of a robot. A server that holds a batch by each
robot's slack asks `slack.Aligner` how long the open batch may wait and which requests are dispatched first:
[`docs/slack.md`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/slack.md) has the rules and a loop.

## Measured

- On an A100-40GB, GR00T N1.6 with CUDA graphs answered 24 robots in time where answering one at a time answered 9:
  each robot 20 ms away, on its own clock, under 5% of responses late.
- π0.5 DROID on an A100-40GB answered 12 robots in time, where one at a time answered 6.
- Seating only the robots it can answer in time kept every seated robot on time; a server that seats every robot that
  asks had none on time (π0.5's batch times on an A100, 16 robots asking).

One replica per GPU: one copy of the model answers all its robots, their requests batched.

## When it applies

- A policy whose robots wait for each response leaves no slack, so its replica serves one robot.
- Each robot reports its RTT; without one, 100 ms is assumed.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md

# What do the components save, measured with the tools in this repository?

On a clean link between two cloud machines, an upload that follows a robot's half-second pause took two to three round
trips with the defaults, and one with any of the components that keep the connection from going idle. That held over
plain TCP, over a WebSocket and over Zenoh, at round-trip times (RTTs) from 11 to 101 ms. At 242 ms the pause cost
nothing; under 1% packet loss, BBR kept the window.

Everything on this page was measured on 2026-11-15 with [`bench/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/tree/main/bench), as released. It is one pair of machines
on one night. **It is not a promise for your link:**
[measure yours](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md).

## The setup

- **Two machines** of one cloud provider, in two regions 11 to 12 ms apart by `ping`, each with 2 shared vCPUs and
  2 GB of memory. Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 7.0, CUBIC as the default congestion control, and
  `net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=1`, the kernel's default.
- **One is the server and one the client.** There is no GPU and no model: the far end responds with a few bytes, so
  every millisecond below is the transport's.
- **Longer RTTs are the same link with delay added** where the robot's packets leave
  (`tc qdisc add dev IF root netem delay Nms`).
- **No run inherits another's window:** `net.ipv4.tcp_no_metrics_save=1`, and `ip tcp_metrics flush all` before
  each run.
- **A cell is 40 uploads** after 3 that are not counted (20 in the table of sizes). An upload "took more than one
  round trip" when it took over 1.5 times its run's baseline: the median of small requests on the warm connection.
- **The pause is counted from the response.** After the response to one upload arrives, the client waits (0.53 s,
  or 0.5 s in the table of sizes) and uploads again. The connection has then sent nothing for the pause plus one
  RTT.

## An upload after a pause, over TCP

A 24 KB upload 0.53 s after each response, on a connection first widened with one 1 MB upload
(`bench/client.py --sizes 24k --idle-ms 530 --samples 40 --warm 1m`). Each cell is the median upload in round trips,
and how many of the 40 took more than one.

| RTT | Default | The server pings every 100 ms | The client sends a byte every 100 ms | BBR on the robot's socket | `tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0` on the robot |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12.4 ms | **1.99 (40 of 40)** | 1.01 (0) | 1.01 (0) | 1.01 (0) | 1.01 (0) |
| 21.4 ms | **2.00 (40 of 40)** | 1.01 (0) | 1.01 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.01 (0) |
| 40.5 ms | **1.99 (40 of 40)** | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) |
| 65.5 ms | **2.00 (40 of 40)** | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.01 (0) | 1.00 (0) |
| 81.3 ms | **2.00 (40 of 40)** | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) |
| 100.7 ms | **2.00 (40 of 40)** | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) |
| 242.2 ms | 1.00 (0 of 40) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.01 (0) | 1.00 (0) |

In milliseconds, the default against the server's ping: 24.7 against 12.5, 42.7 against 21.5, 80.6 against 40.4,
130.6 against 65.5, 162.3 against 81.4, 201.3 against 100.9, and 242.4 against 242.3.

**Why 242 ms took no extra round trip.** The kernel halves an idle connection's window once for each retransmission
timeout that passed, and the timeout is about the RTT plus 200 ms. Up to 101 ms, the pause plus one RTT spanned two
timeouts: the window, 28 packets before each upload, was cut to 10, the least it is cut to, and the upload left in two
flights. At 242 ms they spanned one: the window, 36 packets before each upload, became 18, and the whole upload left at
once.

**Why this differs from an earlier measurement at about 101 ms.** With a robot that uploaded on a fixed period of
0.53 s, counted from the start of one upload to the start of the next, the same 24 KB upload took no extra round trip
at about 101 ms: that silence spans one timeout, not two. Here the 0.53 s is counted from the response, which matches
a robot that starts its pause when the response arrives. **At about 100 ms the two ways of counting the same half
second fall on either side of the edge.** A robot's pause, its RTT and its upload's size decide together, and a small
change in any of them can move a link across.

## Larger uploads

Uploads 0.5 s after each response, with no widening first
(`bench/client.py --sizes 100k,500k,1m --idle-ms 500 --samples 20 --modes idle,ping,keepwarm,continuous`). Median in
round trips; in brackets, how many of the 20 took more than one.

| RTT | Upload | Default | The server pings | The client sends | One after another, no pause |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 13.2 ms | 100 KB | **2.98 (20)** | 1.10 (0) | 1.08 (0) | 1.06 (0) |
| 13.2 ms | 500 KB | **2.99 (20)** | 1.23 (1) | 1.24 (0) | 1.15 (0) |
| 13.2 ms | 1 MB | **3.01 (20)** | 1.31 (1) | 1.36 (0) | 1.35 (8) |
| 81.3 ms | 100 KB | **2.99 (20)** | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) | 1.00 (0) |
| 81.3 ms | 500 KB | **3.00 (20)** | 1.01 (0) | 1.01 (0) | 1.01 (0) |
| 81.3 ms | 1 MB | **2.01 (20)** | 1.02 (0) | 1.01 (0) | 1.01 (0) |

At 13 ms, 1 MB takes over one round trip even with no pause at all: at that distance the time to push a megabyte
through is no longer small beside the RTT. That is the link's rate, and none of these components changes it.

## A camera stream

Frames at a fixed rate with no pause longer than the frame period
(`bench/client.py --modes stream --stream 30x50k,10x100k --seconds 10`), at the 12 ms RTT: 50 KB frames at
30 Hz took a median of 1.02 round trips each, none of 300 over one; 100 KB frames at 10 Hz took 1.09, none of 100.
**A robot that streams has no pause that costs a round trip, and nothing here to gain.**

## With 1% packet loss

The 24 KB upload again, with `netem` dropping 1% of the robot's packets.

| RTT | CUBIC, default | CUBIC, the client sends through the pause | BBR on the robot's socket |
|---|---|---|---|
| 22 ms | **2.00 (40 of 40)** | **2.00 (31 of 40)** | 1.01 (0 of 40) |
| 101.5 ms | **2.00 (40 of 40)** | **2.00 (35 of 40)** | — |

**Under loss, BBR keeps the window.** BBR does not set its window by losses, and took no extra round trip at 22 ms.

## Over a WebSocket, and over Zenoh

A 100 KB upload 0.53 s after each response, 40 per cell, on a connection first widened with one 1 MB upload
([`bench/ws_bench.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/bench/ws_bench.py), [`bench/zenoh_bench.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/bench/zenoh_bench.py)). Each cell is the
median in milliseconds and, in brackets, in round trips. Without a component, 40 of 40 uploads took more than one round
trip in every row; with one, none did.

| RTT | WebSocket, as it is | The server pings ([`ping`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/ping.py)) | The client keeps it warm ([`openpi.keep`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/openpi.py)) | BBR alone on the robot's socket | Zenoh, as it is | Zenoh with the keep-alive file ([`lerobot`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/lerobot.py)) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 11.3 ms | **37.6 (3.3)** | 13.4 (1.2) | 12.7 (1.1) | 12.7 (1.1) | **38.1 (3.4)** | 13.9 (1.2) |
| 21.4 ms | **44.4 (2.1)** | 23.5 (1.1) | 22.7 (1.1) | 23.7 (1.1) | **44.8 (2.1)** | 23.2 (1.1) |
| 40.5 ms | **82.4 (2.0)** | 41.8 (1.0) | 41.8 (1.0) | 43.7 (1.1) | **82.8 (2.0)** | 42.3 (1.0) |
| 80.5 ms | **163.8 (2.0)** | 82.8 (1.0) | 82.6 (1.0) | 87.1 (1.1) | **164.3 (2.0)** | 82.2 (1.0) |

What these two columns are:

- **The WebSocket rows use the `websockets` library on both ends**, the library openpi's server and client are built on,
  with compression off as openpi has it. `openpi.keep()` ran on a stand-in for openpi's client: an object with the two
  members `keep()` uses, the connection and `infer`. In the `openpi.keep` column the machine had no BBR to give, so what kept the window was the ping.
- **The Zenoh rows are two Zenoh peers**, one answering the other's requests, with and without the file
  `lerobot.keep_alive_file()` writes, given to both.

## `openpi.keep()` with openpi's own server and client

One closed-loop run with openpi's own policy server (the `pi05_droid` checkpoint, on an L4) and openpi's own client,
with and without `kept = openpi.keep(policy)`. The client ran in a Linux virtual machine (kernel 6.8, default settings,
CUBIC) on a laptop on a home connection; its kernel measured a smoothed RTT of 38 to 66 ms and a retransmission timeout
of about 240 to 270 ms. Each request uploaded 301 KB, and each row is one 45 s episode. "Outside inference" is the time
`policy.infer()` took on the client minus the inference time the server reported (about 195 ms).

| Setting | Outside inference, p50 (p95) | Idle before a request, p50 | Uploads during which the window fell to about half | Retransmissions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| As it is | **181.4** (237.1) ms | 346 ms | 86 of 89 | 25 |
| As it is | **151.9** (223.5) ms | 378 ms | 85 of 89 | 58 |
| `openpi.keep()` | 92.1 (132.9) ms | 65 ms | 0 of 89 | 0 |
| `openpi.keep()`, BBR module loaded | 85.6 (109.8) ms | 80 ms | 3 of 90 | 9 |
| `openpi.keep()`, BBR module loaded | 90.6 (136.3) ms | 78 ms | 2 of 90 | 25 |

Without `keep()` the connection was idle for longer than its retransmission timeout before almost every request, and the
kernel reduced the congestion window before the upload. With `keep()` the idle time just before each request was under
100 ms, and the window fell during 0 to 3 uploads in an episode. With the BBR module loaded as well (`sudo modprobe
tcp_bbr`, after which `kept.bbr` is true), the time outside inference had a median of 85.6 and 90.6 ms.

A later run had a Linux cloud machine run openpi's own client (CUBIC, no BBR) 30 ms from openpi's own server (the
`pi05_droid` checkpoint, on an L4), six 45 s episodes with and without `keep()`, 301 KB per request.

| Robot | `keep()` | Window left, p50 (packets) | Outside inference, p50 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 30 ms away | no | 72 | 91.2 ms |
| 30 ms away | yes | 215 | 37.1 ms |

With openpi's own server on Linux, also load BBR (`sudo modprobe tcp_bbr`, which `keep()` then puts on the connection)
so the window holds across a pause ([`window.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/window.py)).

## Pictures as JPEG with openpi's own server and client

One closed-loop run with openpi's own policy server (the `pi05_droid` checkpoint, on an L4) and openpi's own client,
the robot a simulated arm on a Mac on a home connection, two pictures of 224 x 224 in each request: first as arrays, as
openpi's guide sends them, then as JPEG, each fitted and encoded as `openpi.image_tools` does it, with the server
pinging each connection every 100 ms and decoding the pictures as `openpi.patch()` makes it do. Each row is one 45 s
episode on the same GPU. "Outside the server" is the round trip the client measured minus the inference time the
server reported; the RTT is a TCP echo to the GPU, measured during the episode.

| Pictures | Upload per request | Outside the server, p50 (p95) | RTT, p50 | Frame to answer, p50 (p95) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Arrays | 301.5 KB | 153.8 (270.8) ms | 56.5 ms | 351.8 (468.0) ms |
| JPEG, the server pinging | 18.8 KB | **58.1** (207.8) ms | 37.5 ms | 279.6 (429.6) ms |

The link was faster during the second episode, so take its RTT out: the time outside the server beyond one RTT fell
from about 97 ms to about 21 ms.

## From a Linux client on a home connection

An upload over a WebSocket 0.5 s after the previous response, 16 per cell: the median in milliseconds and, in brackets,
in round trips of that row. The client was the same Linux virtual machine (kernel 6.8, default settings, CUBIC) on a
laptop on a home connection, or the laptop itself (macOS). The server used the `websockets` library, and in the ping
rows it pinged with `ping_interval=0.1`, which is what `ping.websockets_options()` sets.

| Client | RTT | 100 KB | 500 KB | 1 MB |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Linux, as it is | 34.9 ms | **192.5 (5.5)** | 359.7 (10.3) | 467.0 (13.4) |
| Linux, the server pings every 0.1 s | 35.0 ms | 59.8 (1.7) | 271.6 (7.8) | 445.2 (12.7) |
| Linux, `tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0` | 29.1 ms | 57.7 (2.0) | 392.1 (13.5) | 465.4 (16.0) |
| Linux, BBR on the client's socket | 30.6 ms | 60.0 (2.0) | 157.4 (5.1) | 255.5 (8.3) |
| macOS, as it is | 34.2 ms | 89.4 (2.6) | 135.9 (4.0) | 229.2 (6.7) |
| macOS, the server pings every 0.1 s | 33.1 ms | 89.5 (2.7) | 121.0 (3.7) | 247.2 (7.5) |

At 100 KB the idle restart is the cost: with default settings the window was at 38 segments after 547 ms of idle time,
and the ping, the kernel option and BBR each brought the upload to about two round trips. At 500 KB and 1 MB the line's
upload rate and its packet loss were the cost: six 500 KB uploads sent back to back with default settings took a median
of 14.9 round trips, more than after a pause. There the ping and the kernel option changed little, and BBR took 5.1 and
8.3 round trips where the default settings took 10.3 and 13.4. macOS keeps its window through a pause, and the ping
made no consistent difference there.

This is one home line, a virtual machine and 16 uploads per cell.

## Scope of these measurements

- **One datacenter link** for the sections above the last three; those three are from one home connection.
- **One pause.** 0.53 s after the response (0.5 s for the sizes). A robot that sends its next request sooner than its
  RTT plus 200 ms never takes the extra round trip; one that pauses for seconds has its window cut to its floor.
- **One upload size for the first table.** At about 100 ms a 24 KB upload is at the boundary described above, and a
  smaller or larger one may fall on the other side of it.

## Repeat it

On the server side:

```bash
python3 bench/server.py --port 9000
python3 bench/ws_bench.py server 9101 & python3 bench/ws_bench.py server 9102 --ping
python3 bench/zenoh_bench.py server 7447 & python3 bench/zenoh_bench.py server 7448 --keep
```

On the client side (Linux, as root for the first three lines):

```bash
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_no_metrics_save=1 && ip tcp_metrics flush all
tc qdisc replace dev IF root netem delay 30ms                 # a longer RTT: the delay to add; `loss 1%` too
modprobe tcp_bbr                                              # lets a socket request BBR; the default stays CUBIC

python3 bench/client.py --host HOST --sizes 24k --idle-ms 530 --samples 40 --modes idle,ping,keepwarm --warm 1m
python3 bench/client.py --host HOST --sizes 24k --idle-ms 530 --samples 40 --modes idle --warm 1m --bbr
python3 bench/client.py --host HOST --sizes 100k,500k,1m --idle-ms 500 --samples 20 \
    --modes idle,ping,keepwarm,continuous
python3 bench/client.py --host HOST --modes stream --stream 30x50k,10x100k --seconds 10

python3 bench/ws_bench.py client HOST 9101 plain              # as it is
python3 bench/ws_bench.py client HOST 9102 plain              # the server pings
python3 bench/ws_bench.py client HOST 9101 keep               # openpi.keep on the client side
python3 bench/ws_bench.py client HOST 9101 bbr                # BBR alone
python3 bench/zenoh_bench.py client HOST 7447                 # as it is
python3 bench/zenoh_bench.py client HOST 7448 --keep          # the keep-alive file on both ends
```

The kernel option's column is the first command again after `sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0`.
[`bench/README.md`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/bench/README.md) describes what each block sends.

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/parts-for-a-server-you-already-run.md

# Parts for a server you already run

Each part below is one file that goes into a policy server you already run, or next to a client you already use,
without changing the rest of it. A policy written as a class and served with `seq serve` has them on already: the
[Quickstart](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/quickstart.md) starts there. These are for the code you keep.

## On the GPU

```python
from sequence_ai.engine import optimize
from sequence_ai.engine.batcher import Batcher

optimize(model_user, examples_user)                              # faster in place; kept only where outputs match
batcher_user = Batcher(infer_a_batch_user, sizes=[1, 2, 4, 8])   # several robots' requests in one forward pass
action_user = await batcher_user(observation_user)               # in each request's handler
```

| Part | What it does | Read |
|---|---|---|
| `optimize` | Makes a policy faster on its GPU: each speed-up kept only where its outputs on your observations stay exactly the same | [How do I make a policy faster without changing its outputs, and what does each switch change?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-make-a-policy-faster-without-changing-its-outputs.md) |
| `batcher` | Several robots' requests in one forward pass, in the batch sizes the model lists | [Quickstart: batching and replicas](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/quickstart-inference.md), [How many robots can one GPU serve?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md) |
| `slack` | How long each request may wait, from the slack its robot's action chunk leaves | [`slack`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/slack.md) |
| `replicas` | One process per GPU, each running one call at a time; a process that dies is replaced | [Should I run two replicas of a policy on one GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/should-i-run-two-replicas-of-a-policy-on-one-gpu.md) |
| `one_write`, `ping` | Each response in one write, and a ping answered at once, in a uvicorn or a WebSocket server | [What does each network component do?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/components.md) |

[How do I use the inference components with openpi, LeRobot or GR00T?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-use-the-inference-components-with-openpi-lerobot-or-gr00t.md)
says which of them applies to which framework.

## In a server of your own

Keep it, and give the robots a port of their own. `connect()` speaks the robot's stream: one WebSocket (`GET /stream`)
carrying each observation as it is made and each act after them, which `seq serve` answers. A route of your own that
takes a whole observation per request is not what `connect()` sends. Inside an ASGI app of your own, `App(model_user)`
from `sequence_ai.engine.serve` is the app `seq serve` runs: a function, an observation in and its output out, under an
ASGI server that runs WebSockets.

## In a client of your own

Keep that too, and take single components. Each is one file and imports no other component:

```python
import httpx
from sequence_ai.network import window

transport_user = httpx.HTTPTransport(socket_options=window.socket_options())    # BBR and TCP keepalive, where it can
client_user = httpx.Client(base_url="http://YOUR_GPU:8000", transport=transport_user)

warm_user = window.Warm(ping=lambda: client_user.get("/ping"))     # a ping while the connection is idle
warm_user.used()                                              # call it each time you send on the connection
```

Run against this package's server, those lines sent four pings in 0.45 seconds of idle time. One thing `connect()`
does that your own client must do itself: never let a ping and a request run at the same time. An HTTP/1.1 client
that starts a request while a ping is in flight opens a second connection for it, with a new handshake and a cold
window.

[`examples/components/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/tree/main/examples/components) has a runnable file for each component, and
[Components](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/components.md) describes what each one does, what it needs and what was measured.

## With openpi

Three steps on openpi's own server and client; nothing of openpi's is replaced.

1. **On the GPU**, in openpi's repository, add two lines near the top of `scripts/serve_policy.py`, before it makes
   the server, and start it as before, `uv run --with sequence-ai scripts/serve_policy.py --env=DROID`:

   ```python
   from sequence_ai.network import openpi

   openpi.patch()        # openpi's server from here on: a ping each 100 ms, a JPEG picture handed over as its array
   ```

2. **On the robot**, connect with `openpi.connect()`, keep the connection warm with `openpi.keep()`, and fit each
   picture with this package's `image_tools`, which sends it as JPEG:

   ```python
   from sequence_ai.network import openpi
   from sequence_ai.network.openpi import image_tools          # was: from openpi_client import image_tools

   policy_user = openpi.connect("YOUR_GPU", 8000)              # openpi's own WebsocketClientPolicy
   kept_user = openpi.keep(policy_user)
   observation_user["observation/exterior_image_1_left"] = image_tools.resize_with_pad(frame_user, 224, 224)
   action_chunk_user = policy_user.infer(observation_user)["actions"]
   ```

3. **Check that it works.** After a few `infer()` calls with pauses between them, `kept_user.warm.pings` counts the
   pings the server answered while the connection was idle, and `kept_user.bbr` is `True` where the robot's Linux has
   BBR loaded (`sudo modprobe tcp_bbr`).

[How do I run π0 (openpi) on a remote GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-run-pi0-openpi-on-a-remote-gpu.md) says what each line does, and
what it saved on a real link.

## With LeRobot

LeRobot's remote inference runs over Zenoh, and one setting keeps its link from going idle between observations:

```python
from sequence_ai.network import lerobot

path_user = lerobot.keep_alive_file("zenoh-keep-alive.json5")     # an idle link then sends a frame every 100 ms
```

Give the file to both `lerobot-policy-server` and the robot:
[How do I reduce the latency of LeRobot remote inference?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-reduce-the-latency-of-lerobot-remote-inference.md)
has the flags, and what to measure first.

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/quickstart-inference.md

# Quickstart: from `pip install` to a batched response

Two commands and one short file give you five robots sending requests concurrently, their requests batched, and the
model running in its own process. No GPU, no model and no torch are needed for these steps. The output shown is
from the package built from this repository at 0.62.0, on macOS on Apple silicon with Python 3.12; Python 3.10 or later
behaves the same way.

**How long it takes.** The install took 2 seconds with the packages already downloaded, and the file ran in 0.3 seconds.

## 1. Install

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install sequence-ai
```

The last line it prints:

```text
Successfully installed annotated-types-0.8.0 anyio-4.16.0 certifi-2026.10.23 h11-0.16.0 httpcore-1.0.9 httpx-0.28.1 idna-3.20 pillow-13.0.0 pydantic-2.14.3 pydantic-core-2.50.4 sequence-ai-0.62.0 sequence-base-0.8.12 typing-extensions-4.16.0 typing-inspection-0.4.5
```

The inference components import only the standard library. `optimize` operates on a torch model, or a JAX one, and
uses the torch or JAX your model already has.

## 2. Run five robots against one model

Save this as `quickstart_batching.py`. It is [`examples/quickstart_batching.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/quickstart_batching.py).

```python
import asyncio
import os
import time

from sequence_ai.engine.batcher import Batcher
from sequence_ai.engine.replicas import ReplicaPool


def load_user():
    """Runs in the replica's own process: build your model here, and return what one batch of requests runs."""
    def model_on_a_list_user(observations_user: list) -> list:
        time.sleep(0.05)                                   # one forward pass, whatever the batch: your model's call
        return [{"actions": [[observation_user] * 7] * 8, "pid": os.getpid()} for observation_user in observations_user]

    return model_on_a_list_user


async def main_user() -> None:
    pool_user = ReplicaPool(load_user, replicas=1)        # one replica per GPU; devices=[0] sets the GPU it sees
    batcher_user = Batcher(pool_user.run, sizes=[1, 2, 4, 8], wait_ms=2.0)
    try:
        started_user = time.perf_counter()
        # in your own server, each request's handler awaits batcher(observation)
        outputs_user = await asyncio.gather(*(batcher_user(float(robot_user)) for robot_user in range(5)))
        took_user = (time.perf_counter() - started_user) * 1e3
        print(f"5 robots served in {took_user:.0f} ms, as batches of {dict(batcher_user.sent)}")
        actions_user = outputs_user[3]["actions"]
        print(f"robot 3's own response: {len(actions_user)} actions of {len(actions_user[0])} numbers, "
              f"the first {actions_user[0][:3]}")
        print(f"this process is {os.getpid()}; the model ran in {outputs_user[3]['pid']}")
    finally:
        pool_user.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main_user())
```

```bash
python quickstart_batching.py
```

It prints (your process IDs will differ):

```text
5 robots served in 113 ms, as batches of {4: 1, 1: 1}
robot 3's own response: 8 actions of 7 numbers, the first [3.0, 3.0, 3.0]
this process is 73513; the model ran in 73515
```

## What just ran

| What | Why | Component |
|---|---|---|
| Five requests went to the model as a batch of 4 and a batch of 1: two forward passes of 50 ms instead of five | Calls waiting for a model are served in one forward pass; only the sizes you list are sent, because a model is traced, compiled or graphed for the shapes it has seen | [`batcher`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/engine/batcher.py) |
| Robot 3 received its own response, not its batch's | A batch's outputs are split back per call | [`batcher`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/engine/batcher.py) |
| The model ran in another process | A forward pass never blocks your server's event loop, and a replica that dies is replaced | [`replicas`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/engine/replicas.py) |

**The 113 ms is the stand-in model's.** Its forward pass sleeps 50 ms regardless of batch size. What batching gains on
a real model depends on where the model spends its time:
[How many robots can one GPU serve?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md)

## Use your own model

1. **Your model.** In `load_user`, build your model and return a function that takes a list of observations and returns
   a list of outputs, one per observation. `load_user` is defined at the top of a module, because each replica imports
   it in its own process.
2. **Your server.** In each request's handler, `output = await batcher(observation)`. Any async server works; the
   components are independent of HTTP.
3. **Your GPU.** `ReplicaPool(load, replicas=2, devices=[0, 1])` gives each replica its own GPU. On one GPU use one
   replica: [Should I run two replicas of a policy on one GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/should-i-run-two-replicas-of-a-policy-on-one-gpu.md)
4. **Your batch sizes.** List the sizes your model has been run with, and always include 1.

## Then: a faster forward pass, with the same outputs

If your model is a PyTorch model that calls one module many times per run (a diffusion or flow policy's denoiser),
one more call, `optimize()`, replays that module from CUDA graphs. With torch installed:

```bash
python examples/graph_a_module.py
```

On a machine with no CUDA GPU it leaves the model unchanged, and prints:

```text
cuda_graphs: off - this machine has no CUDA GPU
whole_graph: off - this machine has no CUDA GPU
same outputs, byte for byte: True
```

On a GPU it captures the module, checks the outputs against eager mode's byte for byte, keeps what is faster, and
prints the act before and after. [How do
I make a PyTorch robot policy faster without changing its
outputs?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-make-a-pytorch-robot-policy-faster-without-changing-its-outputs.md)

## Where to go next

- [How many robots can one GPU serve?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md)
- [How do I use the inference components with openpi, LeRobot or
  GR00T?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-use-the-inference-components-with-openpi-lerobot-or-gr00t.md)
- [How do I get a GPU near my robot?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-get-a-gpu-near-my-robot.md)
- A step failed: [FAQ](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/faq.md)

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/should-i-run-two-replicas-of-a-policy-on-one-gpu.md

# Should I run two replicas of a policy on one GPU?

No. Two replicas on one GPU (two loaded copies of the model, each in its own process) do not run concurrently: the
GPU time-slices between the two processes. Measured with π0.5 on an L4, two replicas whose calls overlapped each took
2.1 times as long as one alone, so the GPU's throughput was no higher than with one replica. Give each replica its
own GPU, and on one GPU use one replica and batch its calls.

```python
from sequence_ai.engine.replicas import ReplicaPool

# one replica per GPU; load_user() runs in the replica's process
pool_user = ReplicaPool(load_user, replicas=2, devices=[0, 1])
output_user = await pool_user.run(observation_user)  # in a request's handler: off the event loop
pool_user.close()
```

## What was measured

| Setting, π0.5 on one L4 | Each call took |
|---|---|
| One replica | 1 (the baseline) |
| Two replicas, their calls overlapping | 2.1 times as long each |
| Two replicas with the CUDA Multi-Process Service (MPS) enabled | 6 to 9% faster than without it |

One model and one GPU. A model that leaves the GPU idle for most of a call could behave differently; this one did
not.

## What to do on one GPU

- **Batch.** One replica serving several robots in one forward pass:
  [How many robots can one GPU serve?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md)
- **Make the forward pass shorter**, where the model is PyTorch and calls a module many times per run: [How do I make a
  PyTorch robot policy faster without changing its
  outputs?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-make-a-pytorch-robot-policy-faster-without-changing-its-outputs.md)

## What `replicas` is for

- **One replica on each of several GPUs**, each running one call at a time: `devices=[0, 1]`.
- **A model that never blocks your server.** Each replica runs in its own process, so a forward pass does not block
  the server's event loop or hold its interpreter, even with one replica.
- **A replica that dies is replaced.** `ReplicaError` is the model's own error, and its replica takes the next call.
  `ReplicaDied` is a process that has exited: killed, out of memory, or past its deadline. After a few consecutive
  deaths the pool stops replacing, and raises `PoolHalted` once none is left.

`Batcher(pool.run, runners=2)` combines the two components: batches are formed, two run concurrently, one per replica.
[`examples/serve_with_replicas.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/serve_with_replicas.py) does it around a small model.

## One requirement

The function given as `load` (`load_user` above) must be one a new process can import: defined at the top of a
module, not a lambda and not a function inside another. Each replica starts in its own process and imports it by name.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/slack.md

# `slack`

**Scheduling by the slack an action chunk leaves, for one replica of a model: how many robots the replica can serve,
how long a request may wait for a batch, and which requests are dispatched first.**

One file, standard library only: [`sequence_ai/engine/slack.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/engine/slack.py). Apart from `measure`,
which times a forward pass you provide, it runs nothing and sets no timer: the server that owns the batches calls it,
and passes it the current time.

```python
from sequence_ai.engine import slack

table_user = slack.measure(forward_of_user, sizes=[1, 2, 4])  # forward_of_user(n): one forward pass of n requests
play_user = slack.playback(hz=20, valid_len=15, replan_at=8)  # 15 valid steps, the next requested at the 8th
seating_user = slack.Seating(table_user, play_user["buffer_s"] * 1000, sizes=[1, 2, 4],
                             cycle_ms=(play_user["play_s"] - play_user["buffer_s"]) * 1000)
seats_user, over_user = seating_user.seat([("near", 30.0), ("far", 200.0)])     # (robot, its RTT in ms)
```

With forward passes of 80, 110 and 130 ms this gives `(4, ["far"])`: the replica has capacity for four robots, and the
one 200 ms away is the one to move to another replica: its request may arrive as the near robot's batch runs, and
would then miss its deadline. A batch of four fits the buffer of a robot 100 ms away, and four such robots, run on a
clock with these batch times, had every response in time.

```bash
python examples/components/slack.py        # no model and no GPU: the rules on one pattern of arrivals
```

**Terms.** A *request* is one robot's request for its next action chunk. A *replica* is one loaded model, which runs
one batch at a time. A robot's *round-trip time (RTT)* is the time its requests spend outside the server: uplink,
downlink, and the client's own encoding and decoding (`outside_ms` in the code). The *buffer* is the playback time left
in the chunk a robot is executing at the moment it sends its next request. A request's *slack* is what is left of the
buffer after everything the request spends before its response arrives: its robot's RTT, its wait for a batch, its
batch's time and a margin. A response is *late* when it arrives after the buffer has run out. The rules below keep
the margin before that.

## The rules

- **The buffer comes from the policy.** A response has N valid steps at `hz`, and its robot sends the next request at
  step k, counted from when the previous request was sent. At that moment (N - k) / hz of playback is left, and the
  robot sends a request every k / hz (the cycle). Nothing is declared per request and nothing is read from a response.
  If `replan_at` is not given, k = N: no buffer, and no slack.
- **A request's deadline is its buffer, less its robot's RTT, less 50 ms.** The RTT is what the
  robot reports with its request (`outside_ms`, an integer number of ms from 0 to 5000), and 100 ms for a robot that
  reports nothing. A robot that sent its request late reports the playback time it has left (`left_ms`), and that
  value is used as its deadline.
- **Batch times are measured, not estimated.** `measure` runs each listed size once untimed, then three times. `Table`
  keeps the latest 64 forward passes of each size: their p95 is what a batch is taken to last, for waiting decisions
  and on the clock, and their p50 is what it counts for in the load.
  `Served` keeps what a batch took in the server once dispatched, including the handling around the forward pass; a
  size with 8 answered requests is timed by that.
- **Capacity, by latency.** A robot fits the largest listed batch size whose batch answers it in time: the batch's
  time, the robot's RTT and 50 ms, within the buffer.
- **Capacity, on a clock.** A replica runs one batch at a time and robots send on their own clocks, so whether a
  request is in time also depends on the batches it arrives behind. `slack` runs 2, 3 and more robots on a simulated
  clock, as the loop below serves them: from starts spread evenly over every way their requests can fall in a cycle
  (64 for two robots, 128 for more), each until the run repeats or for 48 cycles. A number of robots is within
  capacity when no response is late in any start, and in no start do the batches fill more than 0.9 of a cycle (the
  load: what the batches typically take for each request, with one request from each robot in a cycle). Each episode
  a robot's loop starts again from the moment it is called, and robots' clocks drift, so a fleet can spend a whole
  episode in any of the ways its requests can fall. `worst=False` asks instead for 95% of the responses back in time
  over the starts, each start counting the same. The first number
  that fails ends the count: robots are admitted one at a time, so a replica reaches a number of robots through
  every smaller one. The clock rounds each batch time up by 3% at most and each RTT up to 10 ms, and keeps each
  verdict by them: a server's timings move by a few ms from one request to the next, and rounded they ask a question
  already answered.
- **Each robot by its own RTT.** Robots are admitted nearest first, and robots that fit the same batch size are batched
  together. A replica runs one batch at a time, so each group's batch must still be in time behind the longest batch of
  another group, and the robots are run on the clock each with its own RTT. The robots beyond that capacity, which are
  the furthest ones, are returned as `over_user`. A far robot never lowers the capacity available to nearer ones.
- **The open batch waits for the replica's other robots** until its most urgent request can wait no longer: the
  latest time that request's response may leave, less the batch's time with one more request in it, less 50 ms. It
  waits only for a robot that is admitted to the replica, whose next request is due safely before then (a robot
  sends its next request k steps after its last one; one whose requests have arrived early and late is counted as
  that much later), and whose own deadline allows the batch. It is dispatched immediately when every admitted robot
  has a request in it, or when one of its robots has no chunk executing yet.
- **A far robot's request is dispatched separately, first**, where the whole batch would miss its deadline: in the
  largest listed size its deadline allows, and only where the requests behind it still meet theirs.
- **A far robot's batch waits one control step at most** for a near robot's request that is due as it would run.
  Dispatched immediately, it would make the near request wait behind it for a full batch time.
- **A robot that sends nothing for four of its periods is dropped from the schedule**: no batch waits for it.
- **Where a policy sets `max_wait_s`** (up to 60 s), that wait replaces the buffer, for capacity and for the batching
  delay. Its robot may run out of actions, and waits.

## In a server

`serve()` runs this loop for you. Tell it how a robot plays an answer, and give it an example to time the batches:

```python
sequence_ai.serve(policy_on_a_list_user, batch=[1, 2, 4], example=observation_user,
                  hz=20, action_chunk_valid_len=15, action_chunk_replan_at=8)
```

Each robot's `connect()` then names it on every request and reports its round trip and what is left of its chunk.
The server holds each request only as long as that robot's chunk allows, and seats a robot at its first act only if
every seated robot stays in time however their requests fall. Any other robot gets a 503 that says why. Without `hz`,
no request waits for another: a batch is what waited while the policy ran.
[`examples/fleet_on_serve.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/fleet_on_serve.py) runs four robots in front of it.

For a server of your own, the loop is:

```python
from sequence_ai.engine import slack

aligner_user = slack.Aligner(table_user, play_user, seated=lambda: robots_on_this_replica_user)    # one per replica

aligner_user.arrived(robot_user, now_user, outside_ms=slack.outside_ms(reported_user))  # each request as it arrives
# the open batch may wait this long; 0.0: run it
wait_s_user = aligner_user.hold_s(open_requests_user, now_user)
# indexes to dispatch first; None: all as one
first_user = aligner_user.split(open_requests_user, now_user, [1, 2, 4], free=False)
aligner_user.answered(batch_user, now_user)                                             # as a batch's responses leave
# each forward pass's time, as it is served
table_user.add(len(batch_user), forward_ms_user)
```

`open_requests_user` and `batch_user` are lists of robots, by the names their requests arrive under (strings; a request
with no name is not scheduled). `now_user` is one monotonic clock, in seconds. Call `split` only when a replica is free
to run the batch. `seating.seat(list(aligner.outsides_ms(now).items()))` computes the capacity of a replica from the RTT
each robot last reported; `Seating(..., most=n)` caps a replica's robots (64 unless given; the serving stack this was
taken from passes its largest listed size). [`examples/components/slack.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/components/slack.py) has such a
loop in about fifty lines, on a simulated clock.

| In the file | What it provides |
|---|---|
| `measure`, `Table`, `Served`, `SizeFailed` | the time a batch of each listed size takes, and its GPU memory where the server measured it (`Table.vram_mb`) |
| `playback` | a policy's `hz`, N and k as `play_s`, `buffer_s`, `step_s` (and `wait_s`) |
| `per_replica` | the capacity of a replica whose robots all have the same RTT |
| `in_time`, `on_a_clock`, `starts`, `kept_only` | whether robots with these RTTs are answered in time, over the starts; one run on the clock; the starts a number of robots is run from; on one thread, answer only the verdicts already kept and raise `NotKept` for the rest, so a server's loop never runs the clock |
| `Seating` | `fit`: the largest batch that answers one robot in time; `seat`: the capacity, and which robots are over it |
| `Aligner` | `arrived`, `hold_s`, `split`, `answered`, `left`, `due`, `outsides_ms`, `replay` |
| `outside_ms`, `left_ms` | what a robot reported, parsed as an integer number of ms, or `None` |

## Relation to `batcher`

[`batcher`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/engine/batcher.py) dispatches a batch when it is full, or `wait_ms` after its first call: one
wait for every caller, and no notion of a robot. `slack` answers the two questions that leaves open: how many robots
a replica can serve at all, and, for the requests waiting now, how long they may still wait and which are dispatched
first. They are two components, each used alone. `Batcher` takes a `hold` and a `first` function in place of
`wait_ms`; `serve()` passes it `Aligner.hold_s` and `Aligner.split`, and a server of your own can do the same.

## Measured

The first five were measured with this file, the fifth on a stand-in for a model. The others were measured in the
serving stack it was taken from.

- **The capacity it computes, on a real model.** π0.5 on one L4, in a test server built from this file around the
  model's batched call, with simulated robots: 15 valid steps, the next request at the 8th, 60 s per cell. At 15 Hz
  (a 467 ms buffer; batches of 1, 2 and 3 in 195, 312 and 429 ms) `per_replica` computed a capacity of 2: 2 robots
  had no late response, 3 had 21% and 26%, and 4 had 99%. At 20 Hz (350 ms) it computed 1, and 2 robots had 40% and
  90% late. The server admitted every robot, so the cells above the capacity show what `seat()` prevents.
  `per_replica` then computed the load by a formula. On a clock, as now, those capacities are the same, for robots
  20, 50 or 100 ms away.
- **The capacity, on three models.** One L4, simulated robots of a 15 Hz policy 20 ms away, 60 s per cell, with the load
  computed by that formula. For π0.5 and GR00T N1.6 it computed 2, and 2 robots had no late response (0.4% in one cell
  of eight). For SmolVLA (batches of 1, 2, 4 and 8 in 256, 273, 303 and 377 ms) it computed 8, and 4 robots had 95% and
  97% of their responses late, 8 had 99%. Computed on a clock, the three capacities are 2, 2 and 1.
- **The capacity on a clock, on a model.** SmolVLA on one L4 again, the same policy and test server, simulated robots
  about 30 ms away. The clock gave a capacity of 1, by the load: two robots' batches fill more than 0.9 of a cycle
  where each request runs alone. Two robots, one more than the capacity, had no late response in 226 (their
  requests 150 ms apart, 60 s) and none in 1,125 (270 ms apart, 300 s; a median latency of 278 ms in the first third
  of that run and 279 ms in the last). Three robots had 5.3% of their responses late where they started together
  and 28.7% where they started evenly spread. Where the server asked `Seating.seat()` as each robot connected, it
  admitted one and refused the next two. One run per cell.
- **A batch held for a robot that arrived just after it had to go.** The same run, SmolVLA, two robots whose requests
  were 150 ms apart: the first request was held 115 ms for the second, which arrived 35 ms after the batch had to go,
  and 55 of the second robot's 56 responses were late. None was late in a server that held no batch. A batch waited
  for any robot that could arrive in time at the earliest, one control step sooner than it does. It now waits for a
  robot whose request is due in time. Rerun on the model after the change, two robots 150 ms apart had no late
  response in 226, and the least any response had to spare was 79 ms.
- **A batch held for a robot whose requests arrive a little early or late.** A stand-in for the same model on a laptop
  (each batch sleeps the model's time), two robots, 120 s per cell: 2 of 512 responses were late where their requests
  were up to 119 ms apart, none of 267 where they were 150 ms or more apart, and 31 of the second robot's 113 where
  they were 120 to 149 ms apart, just past what the first request could wait. The rule then took a robot's next
  request to be due three times the spread of its arrivals earlier, so a batch was held for a request that came just
  after it had to go. It now takes it that much later. On a clock with requests arriving 5 ms early or late (standard
  deviation), two such robots had 6.4% of their responses late before, and 0.02% after. Two robots further apart ran
  120 s at a load of 0.95 with no late response in 445.
- **Four robots on one replica for two minutes**: 20 Hz, 15 valid steps, the next request at the 8th (a 350 ms
  buffer), a stand-in model on a CPU. With every robot assumed to have a fixed 100 ms RTT and a batch timed
  by its forward pass alone, 459 of 1,114 responses arrived after their robot had run out of actions. A request
  waited a median 58 ms for a batch, took 197 ms more in the server and about 131 ms outside it: 386 ms against 350.
  Per-robot RTT and batch times as served were added because of that.
- **Load.** Four robots, 300 s and about 2,100 requests per run: a stand-in on a CPU paced like a 15 Hz policy (15
  valid steps, the next request at the 8th: a 467 ms buffer, 533 ms between a robot's requests; batches of 1, 2 and 4
  in 234, 254 and 299 ms). All four on one replica, two batches of two in each 533 ms and a load of 0.95, had 85.7%
  of their responses back within the 467 ms. Two per replica on two replicas, two batches of one and a load of 0.88,
  had 94.1%, on the slower network of the two runs. `LOAD_MAX`, 0.9, is set from those two runs.
- **Capacity set by the furthest robot.** A replica that had capacity for four robots reported a capacity of one once
  a far robot was on it, and the three robots on it were not answered in time. Per-robot admission was added because
  of that.
- **Dispatching a far robot separately**, a simulation of one replica (15 Hz, a 467 ms buffer, a batch of one
  234 ms, 120 s per run): a robot 60 ms away, beside one 300 ms away, was answered in time 80% and 83% of the time in
  two runs, and 88% and 92% once the far robot's request was dispatched separately. In a third run the replica was
  too loaded for the two and neither was answered in time, either way.
- **A near robot behind a far robot's batch.** On a replica with two robots (15 Hz, a 467 ms buffer, batches of 1
  and 2 in 230 and 250 ms), a robot 23 ms away beside one 250 ms further ran out of actions 31 times in 240 s, and
  not once alone. The one-step wait was added because of that; its effect afterwards is not recorded here.

## Where it helps

- **Several robots on one replica, and a policy that leaves slack** (k < N). The slack is spent on fuller batches: in
  the example, two near robots are answered as one batch of two instead of two forward passes, and still have time
  to spare.
- **Robots at different distances.** A far robot is batched by its own deadline, is dispatched ahead of a batch that
  would make it late, and is the one named to move. The near ones keep their batch size and their capacity.
- **Before any robot connects.** A timing table and a policy's three numbers give a replica's capacity without a
  trial: `slack` runs the fleet on a simulated clock, and
  [`examples/fleet_on_a_clock.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/examples/fleet_on_a_clock.py) prints what each number of robots gets.

## Rules and requirements

- **No slack, nothing to wait in.** A policy whose robot sends a request only when a chunk is fully executed (k = N)
  has no request held, and a replica serves one of its robots. `max_wait_s` changes that only by making the robot
  wait.
- **Each robot reports its RTT**; without one, 100 ms is assumed.
- **One robot per replica** has nothing to batch with.
- **A replica is filled to at most 0.9 of a cycle**, which keeps its responses from queuing.
- **A request due at the very instant its batch must go.** Batch times, RTTs and a cycle that add up exactly leave
  that choice to the last bit of a sum. The clock then takes one of the two ways a real server, whose timings vary,
  would alternate between, and the capacity is that of the way it took.
- **Compute the capacity ahead of time**, when a timing table or a robot's RTT changes: it takes from about 5 ms
  for 2 robots to about 7 s for 32.
- **Robots at different distances are admitted for their worst arrival pattern**, the safe side.
- **`slack` computes who fits**; moving robots and starting replicas is the platform's job.

## Related work

Scheduling several robots' requests by the slack of their action chunks is also the subject of published work, among
it *Action Chunk Scheduling for Batched Robot Policy Serving* (the Armory system, arXiv:2608.00337) and *FirmVLA:
Sequence-SLO Serving for Heterogeneous VLA Fleets* (a NeurIPS 2026 workshop paper). This file is the version General
Sequences serves with. It has not been compared with either.

## Constants

| Constant | Value | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `MARGIN_MS` | 50 | the margin kept between a response and its robot's deadline |
| `ROUND_TRIP_MS` | 100 | the RTT assumed for a robot that has not reported its own |
| `LOAD_MAX` | 0.9 | the largest share of a cycle a replica's batches may fill |
| `MAX_ROBOTS_PER_REPLICA` | 64 | the most robots a replica serves, however fast it is |
| `CLOCK_CYCLES`, `CLOCK_WARM` | 48, 8 | the cycles a start is run for on the clock, and how many of the first are not counted |
| `CLOCK_STARTS` | 128 | the starts a number of robots is run from on the clock; half as many for two robots |
| `IN_TIME_MIN` | 0.95 | with `worst=False`, the share of a fleet's responses that must be back before their buffer runs out, over the starts; by default none may be late in any start |
| `CLOCK_BITS`, `CLOCK_RTT_MS` | 6, 10 | the clock's resolution: a batch time rounded up to 6 significant bits (3% at most), an RTT up to 10 ms |
| `WINDOW` | 64 | the runs kept for each batch size |
| `RUNS` | 3 | the timed runs of each size, after one untimed |
| `SERVED_MIN` | 8 | the answered requests after which a size is timed by what its batches took |
| `OUTSIDE_MAX_MS`, `LEFT_MAX_MS` | 5000, 600000 | the largest values a robot may report for its RTT, and for the playback time it has left |
| `WAIT_MAX_S` | 60 | the longest `max_wait_s` |
| `GONE_PERIODS` | 4 | the periods of silence after which a robot is dropped from the schedule |
| `PERIOD_WEIGHT` | 0.2 | the weight of a new gap between a robot's requests in its estimated period |
