Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/what-is-on-by-default.md

# What is on by default, and how do I turn each part off?

Everything on this page is on as soon as the GPU runs `seq serve` and the robot runs `sequence_ai.connect(url)`:
nothing needs to be added. The last column of each table is how to change a part.

```bash
seq serve                                                  # on the GPU, in the policy's folder
```

```python
policy_user = sequence_ai.connect("http://YOUR_GPU:8000")  # on the robot
```

## On the GPU: `seq serve`

| Part | What it does by default | To change it |
|---|---|---|
| The policy's thread | The policy runs on one thread of its own, one call at a time. Acts that arrive meanwhile wait their turn, in order; pings and uploads are not held behind it | always on |
| Batching | Off: one observation per call | `@seq.concurrent(sizes=[1, 2, 4, 8])` on `@seq.infer`: it takes the observations waiting, stacked, and returns a row for each |
| Addresses | Every address of the machine: `0.0.0.0`, and `::` where it has IPv6 | `seq serve --host 127.0.0.1`: this machine only |
| The robot's stream | Each robot's observations and acts on one WebSocket (`GET /stream`), each message answered as a request; `X-Seq-Act-Formats` names it on every response | always on |
| Observations | Kept by episode, in order; a robot's `Video`, `Depth` and `Tactile` items turned back into the arrays they were. One that did not come is asked for again, and the act waits for it | always on |
| Ping | `GET /ping` is answered at once: `503` with `Retry-After` until the warm-up is done, then `200` with what the server is, as JSON (`server`, `version`, `up_s`, `pid`, `policy`) | always on |
| Identity | `X-Seq-Server: sequence-ai/<version>` on every response, so a robot can tell `seq serve` from another program at its address | always on |
| Warm-up | With `@seq.sample`, the policy runs on its first observation twice at each batch size before `/ping` says ready; `GET /example` hands it out | leave out `@seq.sample` |
| Inputs | The observation as the robot made it, numpy arrays as arrays, each the policy's own to write into | always on |
| Outputs | torch tensors and JAX arrays are sent as numpy arrays (bfloat16 as float32), copied on the policy's thread | always on |
| One write | Each response leaves the server in one write | always on |
| Server time | Each act's answer says how long the server took (`perf`: `handler_ms` from the act's last byte to its answer, `inference_ms` the policy call's), so the robot does not count it as the link's | always on |
| Recording | The last minute of the robots' steps kept in memory, for a recorder to read as they come (`GET /record`, `python -m sequence_ai.network.record`) | always on |
| Token | None, unless `$SEQ_SERVE_TOKEN` is set | `seq serve --token …`, or `SEQ_SERVE_TOKEN=…`: every request and every robot's stream must carry `Authorization: Bearer …` |
| Idle connections | Kept open 5 minutes | always on |
| Size | A request's body, or a message of a robot's stream, up to 64 MB | `limit=` |

## On the robot: `connect()`

| Part | What it does by default | To change it |
|---|---|---|
| The stream | Every observation and act on one WebSocket to the server, kept open: each observation sent as it is made, each act naming how many came before it | always on |
| Video | A `sequence_ai.Video` item goes as low-latency video (H.264), a keyframe every second and after anything lost | always on |
| Pictures | A picture you did not mark (a numpy array H×W×3 of uint8, each side 32 pixels or more, under any key) goes as a video keyframe of its own, lossy, decoded alone | `pictures="exact"`: every byte as it is |
| Depth and touch | A `sequence_ai.Depth` item goes losslessly; a `sequence_ai.Tactile` image as high-quality video | always on |
| Compression | Large arrays are compressed where that saves upload time | always on |
| Lost and refused | An observation the server lost is sent again; one it refused is left out, and the video's next frame is a keyframe | always on |
| Pings when idle | A ping on the stream after each 100 ms of idle time, from the first observation until 60 s after the last observation or act | always on |
| BBR and TCP keepalive | Requested on the stream's socket, where the machine allows them | always on |
| Machine checks | On Linux, one warning when Wi-Fi power saving is on, and one when the machine restarts its window after a pause | always on |
| Token | None | `token="…"`: sent as `Authorization: Bearer …` to a server started with one |
| Two uplinks | Off: one stream, by the default route | `lines=["eth0", "wwan0"]`: a stream by each interface, every observation and act on every line, the first answer used ([how](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-send-each-act-over-two-uplinks.md)) |

`sequence_ai.connect(url, ...)` opens the stream with every default, and takes `token=`, `lines=`, `pictures=` and
`timeout_s=`.

## Check what is on

```bash
python -m sequence_ai.check http://YOUR_GPU:8000
```

Against the [Quickstart](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/quickstart.md)'s server on a Mac, it printed:

```text
sequence-ai check: http://127.0.0.1:8000

  ok  server              sequence-ai 0.64.1, pid 68489, up 9 s, policy QuickstartPolicy_user.infer_user; it answers /ping with 200 and takes the robot's stream (x-seq-stream/3)
  ok  round trip          0.3 ms for a ping on a kept connection (median of 10); 0.0 ms for a TCP connect
  ok  send window         macOS keeps a connection's send window through pauses
  --  BBR                 macOS has no BBR, and needs none for the window
  --  Wi-Fi power saving  not checked: macOS gives nothing to read it from; this machine's requests go over Wi-Fi (en0), and a wired connection takes the question away
  ok  pings when idle     connect() pings after each 100.0 ms of idle time, and the server answers /ping with 200: the pings go on the robot's stream, from its first observation until 60 s after its last observation or act, and keep the connection, and the Wi-Fi radio, from going idle
  ok  pings in inference  answered while the model ran: 0.4 ms against 0.3 ms idle (3 pings in 3 acts)
  ok  server time         the server says it took 0.3 ms of a 1.7 ms act: 1.4 ms outside it, on the network and in this machine
  ok  first act           108.3 ms, the next ones 1.7 ms (observation from GET /example)
```

A `no` line says what is off and why. It takes `--token` for a server started with one, and `--observation FILE` for a
server that hands out no example. It exits 0 when no line says `no`.

## Why each part is on

- **Video, and a keyframe for a picture.** A camera's frames sent as video carry what changed: on our test scene, a
  640×480 camera with a textured background and three moving discs, about 2.5 KB a frame against 921,600 bytes as an
  array. A picture you did not mark goes as a keyframe of its own, about 24 KB a frame there, decoded with nothing
  before it, so a policy asked once a frame, whatever the gaps between frames, reads each as it was sent. Only H×W×3
  uint8 arrays are sent this way: a depth map or a mask goes as it is. A policy that needs its pictures' exact values
  is reached with `pictures="exact"`.
- **Pings.** Linux restarts an idle connection's window, and the next upload then takes extra round trips:
  [Why does my robot's upload get slow after a pause?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/why-does-my-robots-upload-get-slow-after-a-pause.md)
  A ping on the stream is a WebSocket control frame: the server's WebSocket answers it on its own, and an act never
  waits for its answer.
- **The policy's own thread.** A forward pass takes tens of milliseconds, and on the server's event loop it would hold
  every ping and every upload for as long. With a 200 ms stand-in model and two robots, a ping's p50 was 153 ms with
  the model on the event loop and 1.0 ms with it on its own thread. It does not make a robot's act faster: with one
  policy, acts wait their turn either way (p50 316 ms against 320 ms in the same test). What serves several robots
  sooner is batching. CUDA and JAX keep state per thread, so the policy always runs on the same one.
- **Server time.** Without it, a slow model looks like a slow link to the robot.
- **One write.** Behind a tunnel, a response written in two pieces took a round trip more:
  [`one_write.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/one_write.py).
- **Batching is off** because it changes what the policy is called with: a list instead of one observation. Turned on,
  it lets one forward pass serve several robots: one policy took 68.1 ms at batch 1 and 39.6 ms per sample at batch 16
  on one GPU ([`batcher.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/engine/batcher.py)), and
  [How many robots can one GPU serve?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-many-robots-can-one-gpu-serve.md) has what that gains in robots.

## See also

- [How do I serve a robot policy from my own GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-serve-a-robot-policy-from-my-own-gpu.md)
- [Quickstart](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/quickstart.md)

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/what-is-open-source-and-what-is-hosted.md

# What is open source, and what does General Sequences host?

SequenceLink's data plane is open source: the code on the path between a robot and its GPU, which is the policy server
on the GPU, the robot's connection to it, and the components of both, is in this repository under Apache-2.0. It is
the same code wherever the GPU comes from: your own, one rented from General Sequences, or a hosted deployment. The
control plane is General Sequences' hosted service and is not open source: finding a GPU near your robot, starting and
stopping machines, accounts and billing, and building, serving and scoring a hosted policy.

## Open source

Everything a robot and its GPU run, and what a policy is written with:

- **On the GPU:** `seq serve` and the `@seq.policy` decorators a policy is written with, and the inference components
  the server uses, which a server of your own can use as well: `cuda_graphs`, `batcher`, `replicas` and `slack` (`sequence_ai/engine/`).
- **On the robot, and between the two:** `sequence_ai.connect()` and the network components on each end
  (`sequence_ai/network/`), with `openpi` and `lerobot` for the clients and servers of those projects.
- **A policy and an official template, on your own GPU:** the decorators a policy is written with, and `seq init`,
  `seq serve` and `seq weights get`, which run an official template where you choose.
- **Language models:** `sequence_ai.chat()`, with your own key or at a server of your own.
- **Checking and measuring:** `python -m sequence_ai.check`, which says which defaults are on between a robot and its
  server, and `bench/`, which measures what a pause, a ping and a camera stream cost on your link.

A hosted deployment runs the same code: the robot's side of the connection is the same `connect()`, and the GPU's side
is the same server.

## Hosted by General Sequences

What decides where a policy runs, and what it costs:

- **A GPU near your robot.** The closest GPU available to a place you give. How it is chosen is the service's.
- **Machines.** Starting, stopping and billing the GPUs you rent or deploy on.
- **Hosted deployments.** The same policy folder built and served for you, scaled, with benchmarks and evals, and a
  robot driven with it in teleoperation.
- **Your account.** Keys, limits and billing.

The service's client is not in this package: `sequence-cloud` is its own package, and lets `connect()` take a
deployment's name. [generalsequences.com/docs](https://generalsequences.com/docs/) covers the
service.

## On the robot, only what `connect()` is given changes

```python
import sequence_ai

policy_user = sequence_ai.connect("http://your-gpu:8000")   # your own GPU, or one rented from General Sequences
policy_user = sequence_ai.connect("my_policy_user")       # a hosted deployment, by its name, with sequence-cloud
```

## Versions

The version is `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, after [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org). Before 1.0, a minor version may
change or remove an interface, and the CHANGELOG lists each under Changed or Removed. A patch version changes no
interface.

**The hosted platform may need a newer client.** When the service stops accepting an older `sequence-ai`, the entry
of the version it needs starts with "Upgrade to X.Y.Z, as the platform refuses older versions". Your own `seq serve` and
`connect()` are not held to it.

[RELEASING.md](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/RELEASING.md) has what a release is: one
commit, its tag, the package on PyPI and a GitHub release.

---

Source: https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/why-does-my-robots-upload-get-slow-after-a-pause.md

# Why does my robot's upload get slow after a pause?

Because the robot's kernel shrank the connection's congestion window while the connection was silent. On Linux, a TCP
connection that has sent nothing for longer than its retransmission timeout, which is at least its round-trip time (RTT)
plus 200 ms, has its congestion window cut back before it sends again. The next observation then leaves in two or three
flights instead of one, and each extra flight waits a full round trip.

A robot that executes an action chunk and then requests the next one pauses like this on every request.

The fix is to keep the window through the pause. On the robot, `connect()` does it:

```python
import sequence_ai

policy_user = sequence_ai.connect("http://YOUR_GPU:8000")  # BBR where the machine allows it, and a ping while idle
```

Or change one setting on the robot, as root, and keep your own client:

```bash
sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0     # the kernel stops restarting the window
sudo modprobe tcp_bbr                                    # or: load BBR, which window.socket_options() then uses
```

To see whether your robot's machine does this at all:

```python
from sequence_ai.network import window

window.restarts_after_idle()     # True on Linux with the default setting; False where it cannot be read
window.check()                   # warns once, with both fixes, and changes nothing
```

## It depends on the link: measured

A robot sending a request every 0.53 s with 24 KB of frames (19 packets), 40 requests per cell. Two Linux machines,
kernels 6.8 and 7.0, an HTTP server, the RTT set with netem. Each cell is how many of the 40 requests took one extra
round trip.

| Setting on the robot | about 21 ms | about 101 ms | about 241 ms |
|---|---|---|---|
| default | 40 of 40 | 0 of 40 | 0 or 1 of 40 |
| `tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0` | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| a small request about every 100 ms between requests | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| BBR as the system's default | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| default, 1% loss throughout | 39 or 40 | 39 or 40 | 38 |
| default, request size varying by up to 8% (kernel 6.8 only) | — | 19 of 40 | 10 of 40 |

On the short link every request took an extra round trip: its upload took a median of 21.5 ms to arrive, against 0.5 to
1.4 ms with any of the three fixes. On the two longer links the pause cost nothing until the link lost packets or the
request size varied.

**Why the short link took the extra round trip and the long ones did not.** The window is halved once for each timeout
the connection sat idle, down to 10 packets. A 0.53 s pause spans two timeouts at an RTT of about 21 ms, so a window of
29 packets became 10, and a 19-packet upload no longer fit in one flight. At about 101 and 241 ms the same pause spans
one timeout: 38 packets became 19, which just fits. A larger upload, or a longer pause, moves that line.

**The same upload, with the half second counted from the response.** Measured again with the tool in
[`bench/`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/tree/main/bench), which waits 0.53 s after each response before it uploads again, between two cloud machines: every
one of 40 uploads took one extra round trip at 12, 21, 41, 65, 81 and 101 ms, and none at 242 ms. With the server
pinging, the client sending a byte, BBR on the robot's socket or the kernel option at 0, none took an extra round trip
at any RTT. The table above had a fixed 0.53 s from the start of one upload to the start of the next: at about 101 ms
that silence spans one timeout, and half a second after the response plus one RTT spans two. **At about 100 ms, how a
robot's pause is counted decides whether it takes the extra round trip.**
[What do the components save?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md) has the table.

**Larger uploads.** After 500 ms of silence, uploads of 100 KB, 500 KB and 1 MB each took 3.0 round trips. With the
server pinging every 100 ms they took 1.1, 1.1 and 1.25; sent one after another with no pause, 1.05, 1.1 and 1.3.
Three machines of one cloud provider, RTTs of 11.7 and 69.2 ms, 20 samples per cell.

## When it applies

- **For a large upload on a lossy line, use BBR:** 5.1 and 8.3 round trips, against 10.3 and 13.4 by default
  ([the table](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/measurements.md#from-a-linux-client-on-a-home-connection)).
- **macOS.** On macOS the window does not shrink after a pause, so nothing is needed there.

## Four ways to keep the window, and what each cannot do

| Way | Needs | Keeps a window that the pings do not fill |
|---|---|---|
| BBR on the connection: `window.socket_options()`, `window.keep(sock)` | Linux with the `tcp_bbr` module loaded | yes |
| `net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0` | root on the robot | yes |
| A ping from the robot while idle: `window.Warm`, which `connect()` uses | nothing | no |
| A ping from the server: [`ping`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-keep-a-websocket-policy-servers-connection-warm.md) | a WebSocket server | no |

A ping keeps the connection from counting as idle. It does not stop Linux from shrinking a window that the traffic
does not fill, which small pings between large uploads do not. BBR and the kernel setting keep that window as well.
`connect()` requests BBR and pings, so it has both where the machine allows BBR.

Where the machine has no BBR and the policy takes longer to answer than the timeout, no ping can keep the window: load
BBR, or set `net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle` to 0, as the table above says.

The ping interval must be shorter than the timeout. On a link of 11.7 ms, pings 190 ms apart still kept the window
(1.18 round trips for an upload after a pause) and pings 250 ms apart did not (2.04). Anything from 25 to 190 ms
apart measured the same. The components ping every 100 ms.

## Two other things a pause can cost

- **Wi-Fi power saving.** With it enabled, a Wi-Fi adapter sleeps between the access point's beacons, and the
  response to the robot's first packets is delayed until the adapter wakes. `wifi_power.check()` detects it and
  reports how to disable it.
- **A connection the network forgot.** A home or office router can drop its record of a silent connection, and the
  next send is dropped until it times out. TCP keepalive, which `window.socket_options()` enables, detects that
  before the robot's next send does.

## See it on your own link

```bash
python3 bench/server.py --port 9000                                                      # where the GPU is
python3 bench/client.py --host GPU_ADDRESS --sizes 24k --idle-ms 530 --samples 40 --modes idle,ping,keepwarm --warm 1m
python3 bench/client.py --host GPU_ADDRESS --sizes 24k --idle-ms 530 --samples 40 --modes idle --warm 1m --bbr
```

The `x rtt` column reports how many round trips each upload took. `idle` near 2 with `keepwarm` near 1 is this problem,
and the components fix it. All near 1 means your link does not have it.
[How do I measure the link between my robot and my GPU?](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/docs/how-do-i-measure-the-link-between-my-robot-and-my-gpu.md)
explains every column.

## Sources

The measurements are from [`bench/README.md`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/bench/README.md) and the docstrings of
[`window.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/window.py) and [`ping.py`](https://github.com/General-Sequences/sequence-ai/blob/main/sequence_ai/network/ping.py), which also name the
kernel code that does it (`tcp_cwnd_restart` and `tcp_cwnd_validate` in `tcp_output.c`, RFC 5681 section 4.1 and RFC
2861). The table for a robot sending a request every 0.53 s was measured with an earlier version of the tool in
`bench/`.
